title: Enzo Maresca claims Bruno Fernandes deserved to be sent off alongside Phil Foden in derby win
description: The Manchester City manager suggested that the United captain also deserved to see red for kicking out at Foden
fullText:
Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca believes Bruno Fernandes should have been sent off alongside Phil Foden in the first half of his side's 1-0 win in the Manchester derby.

Foden was given a straight red card for lashing out at Fernandes with a wild kick in the 23rd minute after the Manchester United captain had fouled him.

Fernandes also appeared to aim another kick at Foden's back after the initial foul, sparking the reaction from the City man that eventually got him sent off.

However, Fernandes received no punishment for the foul or the second kick, and VAR backed up the original decision made by referee Michael Oliver, with official Matt Donohue confirming: "That looks like a clear red card to me. Looks to be a secondary movement."

Speaking on Sky Sports, commentator Gary Neville said that he was "surprised that Fernandes has got away without a booking", while former United midfielder Roy Keane said that the Portuguese "is the one who is violent here".

And City boss Maresca was also clearly confused by the decision, suggesting that Fernandes should also have seen red if Foden did.

"It can be a red card [for Phil Foden], but I think in the same action it can be a red card for Bruno [Fernandes], in the same action," explained the City manager. "So, anyway... It is what it is. Red card for us. We won," he added.

The sending off did not impact the result negatively for City in the end as the 10 men earned a memorable victory on the road, though Erling Haaland's winning goal was another contentious decision on a dramatic afternoon at Old Trafford.

The result leaves City second in the Premier League after four games, with themselves and Arsenal the only two teams to hold a 100 percent winning record so far.

Maresca's side host Norwich City in the League Cup in their next game on Thursday, before facing Sunderland at the Etihad on Sunday, 20 September in the final game before the international break.

title: Report: Rams DL Myles Garrett to undergo knee surgery
description: Garrett was a non-factor in Week 1 against the 49ers. Now we know why. He's heading to IR after arthroscopic knee surgery.
fullText:
The San Francisco 49ers played well on Thursday in their 27-7 victory over the Los Angeles Rams. So good, the Rams' recently acquired defensive lineman, Myles Garrett, didn't show up on the stat sheet.

Well, we may have an answer as to why: reports say Garrett will undergo arthroscopic knee surgery and be placed on injured reserve. The minimum amount of time for a player to be on IR is four games, so Garrett will be out at least that long.

This didn't begin during the game; Garrett was reportedly dealing with lower-leg and knee issues during Rams training camp, and those probably carried into the regular season. Something was obviously up during the game. The broadcast often cut to the sideline to show Garrett standing and watching the defense on the field, which, given the Rams' predicament, would be strange.

Normally we wouldn't be talking about Rams players and their injuries, but it's Myles Garrett, and the 49ers just got done playing their rivals. The Rams acquired Garrett in a trade with the Cleveland Browns in the 2026 offseason in exchange for a 2027 first-round pick, a 2028 second-round pick, and a 2029 third-round pick. That's a lot of draft capital for a player going to IR after one game, and 49ers fans know this all too well.

The Rams also brought Aaron Donald out of retirement. The thought was that Donald and Garrett together on the field would make an unstoppable pass rush. At this point, we've seen a limited sample size of Garrett, and Donald hasn't suited up yet. The 49ers don't see the Rams again until Week 14.

The Rams host the New York Giants for Week 2, and a Garrett injury may level the playing field.

title: Core injury ends Rafael Devers' season at 37 home runs
description: Rafael Devers' season is over after the Giants placed him on the 60-day injured list with a lingering core muscle injury.
fullText:
Just as his first full season in San Francisco was reaching historic heights, Giants slugger Rafael Devers' year is over with 13 games remaining.

The Giants placed Devers on the 60-day injured list Sunday, Sept. 13 with a core muscle injury that has dogged him for much of this season. The club said Devers, who turns 30 next month, will be examined by specialist William Meyers in Philadelphia on Monday and will undergo a procedure the following day if deemed necessary.

Devers certainly went out with a bang: He hit his 37th home run Saturday at Oracle Park against the San Diego Padres, one day after hitting a grand slam. He hit 11 home runs in his last 18 games.

Devers finished the season with 37 home runs, his most since hitting a career-high 38 in 2021. His .865 OPS and .258/.340/.525 line marked a significant leap from his first half-season in San Francisco, when he batted .236 with an .807 OPS following a trade from Boston to pitcher-friendly Oracle Park. He also drove in 98 runs.

More significantly, he's firmly reestablished himself as the player upon whom the Giants can build around. And that's a significant lift, as the Giants have posted a 62-87 record in manager Tony Vitello's first season.

More: Inside MLB's high-stakes labor war: Will we have baseball in 2027?

title: Rafael Devers placed on the IL, Scott Bandura called up
description: The quest for 40 ends.
fullText:
Rafael Devers' brilliant season has come to a close, as has his quest for 40 home runs. On Sunday, ahead of their series finale against the San Diego Padres, the San Francisco Giants announced that their star slugger is headed to the Injured List with a season-ending core muscle injury.

According to the Giants, Devers has been dealing with the injury for most of the season, and will meet with a specialist. Like Matt Chapman, who also had a core muscle injury, Devers could be headed for surgery, though he should have plenty of time to heal up before Spring Training.

Devers ends his first full season with the Giants with a stunning .258/.340/.525 slash line, good for a 135 wRC+ and 3.4 fWAR. Those numbers are even more stunning when you remember just how bad he was slumping to start the season; but since May 1, Devers has been third among all qualified Major League hitters in both OPS (.953) and wRC+ (157). He trails only MVP favorites Pete Crow-Armstrong and Yordan Alvarez in both categories, and also is eighth in the Majors in fWAR during that time (4.1).

The injury will keep Devers from achieving a trio of notable benchmarks, as he ends the year with 37 home runs, 36 doubles, and 98 runs batted in.

Taking Devers' spot on the roster is outfielder Scott Bandura, who has been called up for his MLB debut. No additional corresponding move was made, as Devers was placed on the 60-Day IL to create a 40-man roster spot for Bandura.

Bandura, who was drafted by the Giants in the seventh round in 2023, has had a spectacular breakout season. The 25-year old lefty, who played college ball at Princeton, started the year with AA Richmond, but was promoted to AAA Sacramento early in the year. After a slow start with the River Cats, Bandura caught absolute fire, and ends his AAA tenure having hit .318/.398/.492 (134 wRC+) with 10 home runs in 94 games. Bandura played quality defense at all three outfield spots with Sacramento, and stole 24 bases in 26 attempts. While this move makes the Giants roster even more crowded — they have 56 players on the 40-man roster — Bandura had played his way into Rule 5 protection, so he was going to need to be added to the roster in the coming months regardless.

Many fans will be wondering why the Giants opted for Bandura over Bo Davidson, but Davidson suffered a mild injury a few games ago after fouling a pitch off his foot.

title: Bengals rookie defensive tackle Landon Robinson has awesome pregame Week 1 outfit
description: Bengals rookie Landon Robinson showed up to Paycor Stadium in his Navy uniform.
fullText:
Cincinnati Bengals rookie defensive tackle Landon Robinson spent his collegiate career at Navy before he was drafted in the seventh round of the 2026 NFL Draft.

His family grew up as Bengals fans, so this was a dream come true. He was great in the preseason, finishing with four sacks and 10 pressures. He led the NFL in both categories going into the regular season.

MORE: Derrick Henry moves up NFL's all-time rushing touchdown list

Robinson made the team and showed up at Paycor Stadium before Sunday's game in his full Navy uniform.

Robinson spent three seasons at Navy, finishing his collegiate tenure with 153 total tackles, 18.5 tackles for loss, 14.5 sacks, two forced fumbles, and one fumble recovery. He finished the 2025 season with 64 total tackles, 8.5 tackles for loss, 6.5 sacks, and one fumble recovery.

The Bengals are looking to start the 2026 NFL season on a high note after only winning six games last year. They have missed the playoffs in three straight seasons and haven't made it since 2022, when they lost to the Kansas City Chiefs in the AFC Championship Game.

The Bengals are up 33-20 on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers late in the fourth quarter. You can watch the rest of the game on FOX. Kevin Kugler and Daryl Johnston are on the call.

title: US schools and police warn about viral ‘Cat in the Hat’ trend after teens’ arrests
description:
Disturbing and AI-generated versions of Dr Seuss character have been used to threaten schools and communities
Schools and law enforcement authorities in the US are issuing warnings against a viral “Cat in the Hat” social media trend in which disturbing or AI-generated versions of the Dr Seuss character are used to threaten students, schools and communities.
The latest warnings come as safety concerns increase and several teenagers have been arrested or charged over posts connected to the trend.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Disturbing and AI-generated versions of Dr Seuss character have been used to threaten schools and communities

Schools and law enforcement authorities in the US are issuing warnings against a viral “Cat in the Hat” social media trend in which disturbing or AI-generated versions of the Dr Seuss character are used to threaten students, schools and communities.

The latest warnings come as safety concerns increase and several teenagers have been arrested or charged over posts connected to the trend.

The Cat in the Hat trend originated on Snapchat as images or short videos showing a disturbing version of the Cat in the Hat, often resembling the character played by Mike Myers in the 2003 live-action film, lurking outside homes, schools or on streets at night.

Some footage appears to be AI-generated, while other posts include real people wearing costumes. Additionally, some videos include threatening messages towards specific towns or schools. More disturbing versions named individuals or included lists of supposed targets.

The posts originally circulated in Ireland and the United Kingdom in August 2026 before quickly becoming viral in parts of the United States and Canada, the BBC reported.

Even though social media users view the trend as a hoax or prank, authorities are warning that causing people to fear for their safety could potentially constitute as criminal harassment.

Recently, near Wichita, Kansas, a 15-year-old was arrested after allegedly posting a video on social media that made ominous threats toward students using the trend.

A statement shared by the Hutchinson police department said that during the investigation, officers determined that a 15-year-old Hutchinson high school student created a TikTok account for that community referencing the Cat in the Hat trend. The juvenile was ultimately charged with two counts of criminal threat.

“Threats of any nature are taken seriously by the Hutchinson Police Department and Hutchinson High School. Regardless of whether a post is intended as a joke, it is unlawful to cause others, particularly students, to fear for their safety,” the statement added.

Similarly, in Worth county, Georgia, two students at Worth county high school are facing charges after the school district said they participated in the viral social media hoax.

Both students involved are being charged, and will also face disciplinary action, school officials say.

Due to the potential threats caused by the trend, some school communities have also increased their police presence as a precautionary measure.

In a statement released by the Grand Junction police department in Colorado, it said that it increased its presence at West middle school and Grand Junction high school “out of an abundance of caution” after the circulation of a Cat in the Hat post. The post led to the arrest of a 14-year old student.

As the trend continues to circulate, law enforcement authorities are urging students to report any safety concerns to a trusted adult, school administrator or law enforcement official rather than reposting or sharing the content.

fullText:
Ex-president urged party at closed-door fundraiser to create sweeping framework, from safety ‘slow-down’ to job losses

Barack Obama urged Democrats to prioritize a “public conversation” about AI management and safety in a closed-door Manhattan fundraiser last week.

The comments by the former US president reportedly urged the party to create a sweeping framework for everything from a safety “slow-down” to domestic job losses and children’s wellbeing.

Obama’s comments follow a summer in which a band of rogue OpenAI chatbots hacked the company Hugging Face, towns across the country opposed datacenters and an AI researcher resigned in a viral social media post warning: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

AI leaders have recently expressed agreement that the race for technological superiority should slow, but have also sought to appease investors, whose stake in the technology is predicted to exceed $1tn in 2026 alone.

“Once you are speaker,” Obama said to US House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York-Democrat, at the fundraiser Thursday. “I would strongly urge that the Democrats put together a framework for a very public conversation,” according to a transcript first reported by the New York Times.

“This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous,” Obama said. “If we do get on top of it, I do think it’s beneficial. I genuinely think it’s going to accelerate, for example, drug development in ways that can help us cure diseases. I do think that this can help us figure out pathways for a clean energy future.”

Obama later added: “I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety. Here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this,’” he said according to the Times.

Obama made the remarks as the US closes in on the midterm elections and Congress has taken little action on AI. While prominent Democratic lawmakers, and some Republicans, have called to regulate the technology, Trump has attempted to aid the AI industry by introducing legislation that would ban state regulations (the bill did not move forward). Democrats face an open presidential field in 2028.

One major flashpoint for the midterm elections is datacenters that power AI companies. Both parties have since begun running ads that oppose them, as one of the few issues, “Maga Republicans and liberal Democrats” agree on, according to an NPR analysis.

On Sunday, while on a trip to his Irish golf course, Trump told reporters that a lot of “very negative forces” are ⁠bringing up concerns ⁠about ​AI that “won’t happen”, and that his main concern was that the US remain the industry leader, according to Reuters.

“We’re leading China ​in AI. ‌We’re the ‌most sophisticated country in the world, ‌and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” Trump told reporters when asked if ‌the AI industry should slow down or be ​more regulated.

In the past, Trump has said on social media that anyone who opposes AI datacenters is likely “backwards and poor”.

“The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” he said on TruthSocial two weeks ago.

title: DnDGem Core – looking for developers to test content-aware layouts
description: DnDGem — adaptive drag-and-drop and layout engine for modern applications. - DnDGem/dndgem
fullText:
Drag. Resize. Adapt. Without breaking your content.

Category: Content-Aware Adaptive Layout Engine

Created and maintained by Davide Agosti.

Canonical website: https://dndgem.dev

DnDGem lays out draggable dashboard-style content using content-aware constraints, deterministic solving, and adaptive reflow — so a layout that geometrically fits can still be classified as less useful when content needs are missed.

It is not merely a grid library, a drag-and-drop wrapper, a React-only library, or a dnd-kit abstraction. React is a thin adapter; Core stays framework-agnostic.

See it immediately: https://playground.dndgem.dev/

Integrate it: Quick Start (~10–15 minutes once packages are available to your app). Public page: https://dndgem.dev/docs/quick-start/

Install with dist-tag alpha only (@dndgem/*@alpha → 0.1.0-alpha.4). This is not a stable release; do not treat latest as a stable or Alpha channel.

See Quick Start for the full first-integration guide.

Validated meta-framework environments (not npm packages): Next.js → @dndgem/react; Nuxt → @dndgem/vue; SvelteKit → @dndgem/svelte.

DnDGem is open source (MIT). Development happens in this public GitHub repository. The project is early Alpha (product maturity: BETA-CANDIDATE): APIs may change; this is not a stable 1.0 release. A Beta readiness program is authorized; a Beta release is not authorized. Claim boundaries: Beta Claim & Support Policy.

Current official npm Alpha: 0.1.0-alpha.4 (release notes — PUBLISHED). Install with dist-tag alpha (npm install @dndgem/react@alpha, @dndgem/vue@alpha, etc.) — resolves to 0.1.0-alpha.4. Previous: 0.1.0-alpha.3, 0.1.0-alpha.2 (superseded), 0.1.0-alpha.1. Historical first Alpha: 0.1.0-alpha.0. latest is not the Alpha channel (Core/DOM/React remain 0.1.0-alpha.0; Vue/Angular/Svelte remain 0.1.0-alpha.2 from first-package npm assignment).

Public product home: https://dndgem.dev (see Public site & domain hosting). 

Validated for Public Alpha on Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit (Playwright desktop engines). Mobile / touch are not validated.

Pointer drag and Escape cancel are supported. Focus / consumer ARIA preservation are baseline-supported. Keyboard drag and screen-reader drag announcements are deferred.

Details: Limitations · Alpha API Contract · Release notes

Preferred public playground: https://playground.dndgem.dev/

Provider URL (keep available): https://dndgem-playground.pages.dev/

Discussions is the planned home for usage questions and broader feedback. Category configuration may follow separately.

Requirements: Node.js 20+, pnpm 10.

pnpm test:e2e runs the Alpha browser matrix (Chromium + Firefox + WebKit). Install browsers once with pnpm test:e2e:install. Chromium-only: pnpm test:e2e:chromium.

Quality policy: feature → develop uses the full local Sprint Final Quality Gate (no GitHub CI). develop → master runs full GitHub CI. See Testing Strategy.

See CONTRIBUTING.md and CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md. Security reports: SECURITY.md.

title: One year in making, private/colleberative HTML5-canvas based editor
description: A markdown-based editor that keeps your writing yours — every note stays on your device, syncing directly between your devices over an end-to-end encrypted channel. No cloud. No account. No company reading your words.
fullText:
Open a tab. Open a notes app. Type a half-formed idea, a draft email, a thing you would not say out loud. It lands on a server you do not own, in a city you have never been to, governed by a fourteen-page agreement you did not read. Tasfer refuses that trade.

Public beta. It runs, it syncs, and it will break. Nothing you write here is guaranteed to survive an update.

An app you write in. Notes, drafts, journals stored on your device, encrypted end-to-end in transit, synced device-to-device with no central server and no account.

You would not hand a notebook to someone in the street. You would not read your medical history into a stranger's phone. You would not shout your half-drafted resignation letter into a crowd.

And yet — every free notes app, every free document, every free AI assistant is a trade. Your thoughts, in plain text, on a machine you will never see, indexed by software you will never read, owned by a company that will outlive you or be outlived by you. The bargain is so quiet you forget you took it.

Tasfer does not take the trade. Not the storage. Not the keys. Not the protocol. Not the permission to leave.

On your device. Every keystroke lands in your own storage, instantly — no round-trip, no "saving" spinner reporting back to a server somewhere. Tasfer works on a plane, in a basement, in a Faraday cage.

Between your devices. When you sync, traffic flows peer-to-peer, encrypted with keys that never leave your hardware. Your laptop talks to your phone the way two friends meet — in person, with no third party in the room.

Through a stateless relay — only when a direct path can't be made. It forwards bytes it cannot decrypt. No accounts. No logs. No memory of who connected to whom. It introduces, then forgets. And if you don't trust ours, point Tasfer at your own — it's a config field.

Every keystroke lands in your storage. Not 'syncs to your storage.' Lands. The network is a choice, not a dependency. Pull the plug and Tasfer keeps working.

Documents are encrypted on your device before they ever cross a wire. Only the people you share with hold the keys. The relay is structurally unable to read your work — not 'promises not to.' Cannot.

A postman with no inbox. It introduces peers, then forgets they met. No account database. No message log. No surface for a subpoena, a leak, or a curious engineer to land on.

Every privacy promise on the internet is a sentence on a webpage. Ours is a directory of source files. The encryption is in the repo. The relay is in the repo. The protocol is in the repo. Every line that runs between you and the words you wrote is something you can audit, fork, or replace with a build of your own.

Every commit. Every dependency. Yours to read, yours to change, yours to keep.

Install it. Fork it. Swap the relay. Take it offline for a year. Hand it to a friend. Bury it. Walk away. The choice was always supposed to be yours — Tasfer is the editor that finally agrees.

title: Judge rules Trump administration order to fire FEMA staffers was illegal
description: A federal judge said in a filing Friday that a Trump administration order for the Federal Emergency Management Agency to cut its staffing nearly in half was illegal.
fullText:
A federal judge said in a filing Friday that a Trump administration order for the Federal Emergency Management Agency to cut its staffing nearly in half was illegal.

In a decision that marked a critical victory for union workers in the ongoing lawsuit, US District Judge Susan Illston in Northern California said the Department of Homeland Security "acted arbitrarily and capriciously" when it revoked FEMA's authority to renew contracts for the agency's on-call disaster response teams. She also rebuked officials for deleting Signal messages that could have been used as evidence in the lawsuit.

The Cadre of On-Call Response and Recovery teams, known as CORE, make up about 40% of FEMA's workforce. The teams are often the first federal boots on the ground when hurricanes and other large disasters strike. Many of those workers oversee aid distribution and long-term funding to states and communities.

Traditionally, CORE workers have served two-to-four-year contracts that were almost always renewed. But amid an aggressive Trump administration effort to downsize the federal government in 2025, DHS limited FEMA to renewing these contracts to 180 days at a time while it considered a long-term plan to shrink the agency.

In January, DHS instructed FEMA to let at least some of those contracts lapse to force employees out as their terms expire.

The moves were part of a broader push by the Trump administration to overhaul FEMA, shrink its size and shift more responsibility for disaster response and recovery to the states. Since President Donald Trump took office, his administration has argued that the disaster relief agency is ineffective, partisan and bloated, despite a 2023 Government Accountability Office report that found the agency was facing a staffing shortfall of more than 6,000 employees.

While FEMA is a part of DHS, Congress passed a law in 2006 that stated the homeland security secretary "may not substantially or significantly reduce" FEMA's "authorities, responsibilities, or functions."

Illston noted that DHS was exempt from Trump's January 2025 hiring freeze but the department then interpreted "new hires" under the hiring freeze to include FEMA CORE renewals.

Referring to the DHS decision to revoke FEMA's authority to renew those CORE appointments, Illston wrote, "There is no evidence in the record reflecting reasoned decision for this about-face or for the subsequent conditions DHS placed on FEMA's renewal authority."

A FEMA spokesperson said in a statement the agency "continues to maintain a roster of experienced leadership and support staff across headquarters and regional offices."

"We're ensuring workforce stability and a strong, deployable force for upcoming national events and potential disasters; making the agency leaner, faster and laser-focused on supporting state, local, tribal and territorial partners before, during and after disasters," the spokesperson said.

In a separate filing, Illston said the use of Signal, a secure messaging app with robust privacy features, by former acting FEMA head Karen Evans and former DHS deputy chief of staff Joseph Guy violated federal law and department policy.

Evans created a Signal chat that "would appear to be highly relevant to this case" with the text messages set to auto-delete after four weeks, the judge wrote. In March, after she had been named a defendant in the lawsuit, Evans shortened the auto-delete timer.

Evans created a backup of her Signal messages on April 2026, "by which point the most timely messages were long since deleted," Illston wrote. The court found that Evans' actions were intentional.

"Evans should have known better," Illston wrote. "She previously served as Chief Information Officer at DHS, in charge of the agency's records preservation policies."

The judge barred the administration from relying in future proceedings on any previous testimony that denies the plans to dramatically reduce FEMA staffing or DHS' involvement in the issue.

In those additional proceedings, she wrote, "the Court will presume that the lost Signal messages would have been unfavorable to Defendants because they would have been further evidence of Defendants' plan, DHS's control, and Defendants' implementing actions."

The decisions are a win for the American Federation of Government Employees and the AFL-CIO, the labor unions that brought the lawsuit. But Illston didn't address what remedies the government should provide, ordering the parties to come up with an agreement on the scope of relief.

The unions had sought the rescission of all non-renewal notices sent to CORE employees since the start of the year and to return employees to their positions, along with stopping the agency from implementing a plan to cut 50% of its staff.

But Illston noted that relief would be too broad because FEMA is no longer systemically not renewing the CORE contracts "and there is no indication at present that FEMA is otherwise taking action" on the plan to cut half of its workforce. But the judge said DHS "continues to usurp FEMA's authority" by ordering the agency to offer contracts of up to 180 days.

This story has been updated with additional information.

title: What jobs wipeout? Morgan Stanley says white-collar workers might benefit the most from AI
description: Economists at Morgan Stanley say that veterans of the white-collar labor force actually stand to benefit most from the productivity gains delivered by AI.
fullText:
White-collar workers are said to be highly at risk of job displacement by AI.

Yet, Morgan Stanley says office workers stand to benefit the most from AI-enabled productivity gains.

"AI-related job postings have been targeted towards higher-income consumers," the bank said.

Morgan Stanley has some good news if you're an office worker who lives in fear of an AI-fueled jobs wipeout.

The Wall Street Bank said on Friday that the most exposed demographic to AI disruption stands to benefit the most. As widespread AI-driven layoff announcements have dominated news cycles, white-collar workers across industries have wondered if their jobs are next to be automated away.

But according to Morgan Stanley economist Heather Berger, it's these workers who stand to win from the ways in which AI will reshape labor.

"High-income, college-educated, urban households are most exposed to AI displacement but also to potential AI gains: productivity-driven wage growth, job creation, wealth effects, and disinflation," she wrote. "We think these upside channels are underappreciated."

Berger's team uses the acronym CHIC— college-educated, high-income, city-dwelling. This group, by Morgan Stanley's assessment, is most likely to be impacted by AI as a job-market disrupting force as it continues to evolve.

The economists noted that younger CHIC workers are more likely to see parts of their jobs replaced by AI, particularly routine, entry-level tasks. But older colleagues could end up seeing wage growth due to productivity gains that AI is expected to deliver without fully replacing them.

"In terms of job creation, it is still early, but new AI-related occupations have so far been aimed at these same CHIC consumers," Berger added. "AI-related job postings have been targeted towards higher-income consumers with some experience in similar 'highly-exposed' industries."

The bank's prediction comes as AI fears are on the rise in the job market and beyond, as ominous statements from AI industry insiders and doomsday scenarios have gone viral. But Berger's team maintains that AI job fears may be overblown, and she isn't the only one.

Andrew Slimmon, head of applied equity advisors at Morgan Stanley Investment Management, told Business Insider earlier this year that he wasn't worried about the impact AI would have on employment. He predicted that the market would rebound and become stronger, similar to how the dot-com boom of the early 2000s reshaped the labor force.

Now Berger and her team see a similar scenario taking shape as the evolution of AI transforms the economy in a way that benefits CHIC households, helps create more wealth, and ultimately fuels more consumer spending.

"Overall, CHIC households are more exposed to labor displacement, but also more exposed to productivity-driven wage growth, new job creation, wealth effects, and longer-term disinflation," Berger noted.

title: Chicago mayor bets progressives will turn out for him in announcing reelection bid
description: Progressive Brandon Johnson hopes a growing far-left movement can help him overcome voter dissatisfaction with his job performance.
fullText:
Mayor Brandon Johnson is launching his reelection campaign Sunday despite daunting approval ratings, betting the progressive coalition that helped elect him in 2023 is stronger now than it was four years ago.

The mayor confirmed his plans to POLITICO ahead of the announcement at the DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center on the city's South Side.He plans to argue that his administration has followed through on policies he pitched when he first ran for office and that there is still unfinished business ahead.

"I made a promise four years ago that I would work every day to build the safest, most affordable big city in America by investing in people, and that's exactly what we've done," Johnson said, pointing to investments in affordable housing, infrastructure and mental health clinics, along with declining crime rates.

But the mayor also faces high disapproval ratings, with support for a prospective reelection bid at just 13.6 percent, according to a recent University of Chicago Mansueto Institute poll. He'll also have to take on a field of strong Democratic challengers, including Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias, Rep. Mike Quigley and state Comptroller Susana Mendoza – all of whom tack closer to the ideological center than Johnson.

Along with the ideological fight comes jockeying for cash: Giannoulias, backed by a coalition of labor unions and prominent business and civic leaders, begins the race with a commanding financial advantage of nearly $22 million in campaign funds, whereas Johnson's political operation has less than $1 million on hand, according to the most recent campaign filings.

For Johnson, success may hinge on whether progressive activists can capitalize on renewed energy for their movement, including by likely nabbing financial backing from the powerful Chicago Teachers Union, which helped propel him into office in 2023. (The CTU told POLITICO the endorsement process hasn't yet begun.)

Chicago Democratic Socialists of America Co-chair Sean Duffy said recent victories by progressive and socialist candidates have fueled organizing efforts and created momentum that could benefit Johnson.

"People are tired of politicians who don't deliver and who side with corporations over working-class people," Duffy said. "There's a palpable energy around candidates and organizations that are offering a real alternative." Still, Duffy noted that Johnson now faces the challenges that come with being the incumbent rather than the insurgent candidate as he was in 2023.

Though Johnson is not a member of the DSA, which has made strides with several shocking upsets in primaries across the nation this year, he is widely seen as an ally. His supporters point to recent wins by far-left candidates around the country as evidence that progressive voters could carry him through the election in February and the potential runoff in April.

"It's clear that the progressive energy that we ignited back in 2023 has impacted the rest of the country," Johnson said. "People are tired of corporate greed at the expense of everyday people."

Johnson's first term has been defined by moments marked by mixed public support, such as his handling of the city's response to federal immigration enforcement actions, and challenges, like his repeated battles with City Council as the city faces a projected budget gap of $882 million in 2027.

But while Giannoulias has dinged Johnson for his fights with aldermen and attempted to position himself as a coalition-builder, the mayor doesn't shy away from the conflicts in pursuit of his policy goals.

"If we're fighting over whether we should raise wages for working people or whether corporations should pay more, those are fights worth having," he said. "The city deserves a fighter who's going to prioritize working people."

That message mirrors the priorities of Chicago's DSA chapter, which says its membership has grown to more than 3,200, including roughly 1,000 new members over the past year.

Earlier this year, the group adopted a strategy centered on what Duffy describes as a choice between "tax the rich or austerity."

The local DSA chapter has not endorsed Johnson – or anyone else – in the mayor's race, instead concentrating on City Council contests, where leaders believe they can have the most immediate impact. The chapter has already endorsed six council candidates and plans another round of endorsements later this fall.

The goal, Duffy said, is to elect aldermen who support policies such as stronger tenant protections, public financing of elections and higher taxes on wealthy residents and large corporations to help fund city services.

That effort could help Johnson score more policy wins if he wins a second term. With 50 aldermen on the council, a mayor needs 26 votes to move legislation. Johnson has struggled at times to build that majority, most notably during bruising budget battles that saw aldermen reject his proposal and advance their own version.

"If I'm Brandon Johnson, I'm thinking about 'How do I get to a strong progressive majority?'" Duffy said.

Whether that energy is enough to overcome Johnson's political headwinds remains to be seen. But as he begins his reelection campaign, the mayor is making clear that he has no plans to change course.

"If I don't have that fight, then what's the whole point of me being here?" Johnson asked.

title: McConnell’s return shines spotlight on older lawmakers
description: Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) expected return to the Senate next week is drawing attention again to the health of aging lawmakers. McConnell, 84, was hospitalized over the summer for nearly two month...
fullText:
Sen. Mitch McConnell's (R-Ky.) expected return to the Senate next week is drawing attention again to the health of aging lawmakers.

McConnell, 84, was hospitalized over the summer for nearly two months after falling at home and receiving treatment for pneumonia. He has since been recovering at home and engaging in what he described as an "intensive regimen of physical therapy."

His extended absence and advanced age have reignited conversations about lawmakers staying in office too long, with polls showing many voters support term limits, even as they also keep reelecting elder statesmen.

McConnell was first elected to the Senate in 1985 and is the 10th longest-serving senator in U.S. history. He is not seeking reelection to his current term, which ends in January.

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) has repeatedly raised questions over whether McConnell is fit to serve because of his health challenges this summer.

"I hope that he is one of the reasons that we get term limits. I'll tell you what, I'd even name the bill after him," Beshear told CNN.

Iowa's 44-year-old Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Rob Sand, has voiced his support for both age and term limits.

"The idea is, I want term limits. I want age limits. Let's go get them," he told reporters in April.

Compounding these arguments is the recent spate of lawmakers who have died in office — six in this term alone. Democratic Reps. Raúl Grijalva (Ariz.), Gerry Connolly (Va.) and David Scott (Ga.) were a decade or more past the typical retirement age of 65. Sen. Lindsay Graham (R-S.C.) was 71 when he died in office from aortic dissection — a sudden condition that is not typically screened for — in July.

In 2023, 90-year-old Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.) died while in office.

Rep. Kay Granger (R-Texas) had left office less than two years before her death last month at age 83. The end of her tenure was marred by the revelation that she had been residing in a senior living facility and experiencing what her son Brandon Granger described at the time as "dementia issues." Her family confirmed her death was caused by complications from Alzheimer's disease.

Support for term limits on Congress remains overwhelmingly popular among Americans across the political spectrum.

An NPR/PBS News/Marist poll released in May found that 83 percent of U.S. adults support term limits, with self-identified Republicans showing the highest rate of support at 89 percent. The same survey found that 80 percent of Americans also support an age cap on congressional candidates.

According to Aaron Dukette, senior strategist for the nonpartisan advocacy group U.S. Term Limits, support for imposing term limits has "skyrocketed" among Congress members in the past few years.

"We have 130-plus people who have signed a pledge and gotten on as co-sponsors for our amendment. So, it's not obviously at the two-thirds threshold that you need to have both chambers, but it's certainly growing," Dukette told The Hill. "And I think people on both sides of the aisle started to recognize that this is something that's going to benefit our whole electoral process and not just one party over the other."

The joint resolution supported by his organization proposes limiting U.S. senators to two terms and House members to three terms. The version introduced in the House last year has 115 co-sponsors, 107 of whom are Republicans.

Although conversations and support for term limits and age limits persist among the general public, the discussions are rarer among lawmakers themselves, according to those who've worked with them.

Rodney Whitlock, managing director of Cozen O'Connor Public Strategies, was health policy adviser to Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) until 2015. Grassley, who will turn 93 next week, is now the oldest member of Congress and was among the oldest when Whitlock last worked for him more than a decade ago. Grassley ranks as the longest-serving U.S. senator currently in the chamber, exceeding McConnell's tenure by four years.

"It is not as common as one would think, unless the member starts to have issues," Whitlock said when asked whether lawmakers and their staff talk about age.

He argued that the issue of an aging workforce is a broad one.

"Nobody should be looking at this going, 'This is a unique problem to members of Congress.' No, it's not. It is societal. It is our issues with aging. All of these things are part of this conversation," said Whitlock. He noted that during his time as a congressional staffer, views on aging lawmakers were more respectful, but the discussions have since become "overtly political."

While describing that Grassley sees public service as a "calling," Whitlock said there are "certainly" lawmakers who stay in office simply because they have "grown so accustomed to the lifestyle."

Discussions about American gerontocracy encompass all branches of government. President Trump, 80, is the oldest person to be sworn in as U.S. president; former President Biden became the oldest sitting president, leaving office at 82.

At the Supreme Court, 5 out of 8 sitting justices are past age 65; Justice Clarence Thomas is the oldest at 78.

Dukette from U.S. Term Limits said his organization is focused on limiting congressional service based on terms over age, reasoning that limiting terms would naturally resolve the age issue.

"We understand the concern and the desire for age limits, given the fact that we have many prominent elderly members of Congress that are running into health troubles while still being in office and they go ... missing for a time," said Dukette. "If it wasn't for the 20, 30, 40-year careers that put them in that place in the first place — most members that run for Congress don't start doing so in their 60s or 70s. They do so in their 40s or even in their 50s, and then they're there for decades of service."

When reached for comment on his condition and expected return, McConnell's office referred to the senator's last public statement released at the start of August, in which he said he would "continue my recovery at home" and "continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business."

The Hill has reached out to Grassley's office for comment.

title: Dem handlers lash out when cameraman confronts their boss about debate: ‘No pictures’

title: Mosquito-borne illnesses increasing in US. See map of affected states
description: State and federal officials have warned about surges in multiple mosquito-borne illnesses this season. See which states have been most affected.
fullText:
As Western states fight a rise in West Nile virus and the South contends with a surge in dengue fever, mosquito-borne diseases have left some Americans uneasy as this summer season comes to a close.

While some mosquito-borne illnesses common in more tropical climates, such as malaria and yellow fever, have been absent from the mainland U.S. for several years, many others remain present and are gaining ground stateside. An especially active West Nile season, for example, has prompted multiple state and federal agencies to issue public warnings.

"We're seeing a number of mosquito-borne diseases appear more frequently or in areas where historically they have been uncommon," Dr. Jorge Parada, medical adviser for the National Pest Management Association, told USA TODAY. "Warmer temperatures and longer mosquito seasons can expand the range of certain mosquito species and increase the amount of time they remain active each year."

This year's exceptionally active tick season can be attributed to similar culprits, experts previously told USA TODAY, as warming weather and an increasingly favorable climate allow pests to live longer and travel further.

Even in one of the most biodiverse forests on Earth, mosquitoes are increasingly finding humans on the menu, according to multiple studies conducted in Brazil. Researchers say habitat changes and growing human presence may be making people an easier target than wildlife, potentially increasing opportunities for mosquito-borne diseases to jump between animals and humans.

West Nile cases began picking up earlier this year, with the vast majority recorded in August and September, according to historical Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) data. The CDC said in a July 1 notice that numbers represented a more than 20-year high for that time of year.

"West Nile virus is more prominent this year. National surveillance data from the CDC shows that the season got off to a historically early and active start," Parada said. "The virus appears to have surged earlier in the spring and summer than we typically see, which is likely driven in part by warm weather and active mosquito populations."

West Nile is primarily a mosquito-bird disease, with humans being an incidental host, Parada said. This means mosquitoes get it from infected birds, and people then get it when bitten by mosquitoes. When more birds have the virus, more mosquitoes carry it as well.

Warmer weather that comes earlier and lasts longer enables more mosquitoes to live and bite more people. Additionally, natural cycles in the bird population play a role in year-to-year transmission, Parada explained.

"Because West Nile can be fatal to birds, periods of heavy transmission may eventually reduce the number of infected birds available to sustain the cycle," he said. "Over time, new generations of birds that have never been exposed to the virus become susceptible, creating conditions for transmission to increase again."

As of Sept. 8, the CDC has confirmed 504 total cases of West Nile in 41 states. A large portion, 363, of those were neuroinvasive disease cases: a severe form of the illness associated with high mortality and disability that occurs when the virus spreads to the central nervous system.

The CDC estimates that only 1% of those who contract West Nile experience severe neuroinvasive disease, while 20% develop a flu-like illness that resolves without medical intervention. The majority, or roughly 80%, do not develop any symptoms or apparent illness.

The good news: The large percentage of U.S. cases categorized as neuroinvasive West Nile virus doesn't necessarily mean more people who contract the illness are getting sicker. Instead, it's an anomaly of how we track and report infectious disease in the United States.

"This is most likely due to a diagnosis and reporting bias, rather than a sudden change in the virus itself," Parada said. "Most people infected with West Nile virus never develop symptoms, so they don't seek medical care and are never officially diagnosed. By contrast, patients who develop severe neurologic symptoms are much more likely to be hospitalized and get tested."

Most mosquitoes don't carry West Nile, and the average American who is bitten is unlikely to get sick, Parada said. About 80% of people don't develop symptoms, and most who do experience what's known as "West Nile fever," a flu-like illness that can cause fever, headache, body aches, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash or swollen lymph nodes.

In the rare neuroinvasive cases, the virus can affect the central nervous system and cause serious conditions such as meningitis or encephalitis. Symptoms may include high fever, stiff neck, confusion, disorientation, muscle weakness, numbness, paralysis, vision loss, coma or even death.

As with other infectious diseases, people most at risk include older adults (especially over 60), those with weakened immune systems, and individuals with chronic underlying medical conditions such as cancer, diabetes or chronic kidney disease.

Prevention is the best tool in fighting West Nile, said Parada, who suggests the following:

Use EPA-registered insect repellent. Products containing DEET, picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus, para-menthane-diol and IR3535 have all been shown to be effective when used according to label directions.

Mosquitoes can breed in as little as half an inch of standing water, so remove water around your property. That means regularly emptying water from flowerpots, birdbaths, buckets, tires, toys, pet bowls and other containers. Don't forget to check and clean gutters, which are a commonly overlooked source of standing water.

If mosquitoes are becoming a persistent problem, contact a qualified pest control professional. They can help identify potential breeding sites and recommend a targeted management plan.

While West Nile is making "historic" headlines, other mosquito-borne illnesses have seen surges in the United States this season.

Dengue fever spiked in Florida recently, totaling 111 cases as of Sept. 5. All of those cases were locally acquired, meaning people caught it in Florida, not while traveling abroad. The rise is compared with 2025, during which 62 people tested positive in total.

Like West Nile, the symptoms are generally flu-like, including aches and pains, nausea, vomiting and rash. About 1 in 20 people who contract dengue develop a more serious illness called hemorrhagic fever, according to the CDC, which can entail symptoms like abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums and blood in stool or vomit.

"Diseases such as dengue, chikungunya, and Zika have generated increasing concern in parts of the United States in recent years," Parada said. "Looking ahead, one of the concerns among public health experts is whether mosquito-borne diseases that were once eliminated from the U.S., such as malaria, could eventually gain a foothold in areas where environmental conditions become more favorable."

He added: "All of this underscores the importance of mosquito surveillance, mosquito control programs, and personal protection measures."

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Mosquito-borne illnesses increasing in US. See map of affected states

title: House Speaker Mike Johnson says Trump's $5,000 'dividend' needs congressional approval
description: President Donald Trump's proposal to send $5,000 to every American adult if his Republican Party maintains control of the House and Senate in the November election needs congressional approval, House ...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's proposal to send $5,000 to every American adult if his Republican Party maintains control of the House and Senate in the November election needs congressional approval, House Speaker Mike Johnson said Sunday, while pledging to try to make it happen.

Trump made the unusual pitch at the party's midterm convention in Dallas last week, promising a "Trump Dividend" if voters keep the GOP in power on Capitol Hill. The president later told CBS News Texas that he did not think Congress would need to authorize the payments, though he did not specify how he could spend more than $1 trillion without lawmakers' authorization.

But Johnson, R-La., said congressional approval is needed. "I would assume, yes, he'd need Congress to act, and that's a creative idea," he said.

A few hours later, Trump said he would deliver on his promise. "The 5,000's going to happen, 100%," he told reporters before boarding Air Force One in Ireland, where he attended a pro golf tournament at his resort.

Johnson, meanwhile, said he would work to get Trump's proposal through Congress despite a small Republican margin.

"He's the big idea's president. We're going to try to implement everything we can," he said. "I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that like they have to do everything else."

The dubious election-year gambit could cost more than $1 trillion, putting further strains on the country's nearly $1.8 trillion annual budget deficit and exacerbating concerns of inflation. The economy is confronted by persistent inflation and increasing interest rates, a tough combination for governing Republicans as they seek to hold on to control of Congress.

The president argues that payments would be possible because of the strong economy, but consumer sentiment is weak as gasoline prices rise because of the war with Iran and wages struggle to keep pace with inflation.

Trump told reporters earlier Sunday that the payments would be "easy enough" because the United States has a strong economy.

"We can easily handle that because we're taking in so much money," he said. "We've never done better."

Just one-third of U.S. adults approve of how Trump is handling the presidency, according to a July poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. That compares with 37% in June and 42% who approved of his work when he took office. Majorities also disapprove of his handling of the economy and immigration, issues that were central to Trump's election in 2024.

On Sunday, Trump said the gas price will "drop like a rock" but indicated no deal any time soon with Iran to end the conflicts and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Johnson appeared on CNN's "State of the Union" and NBC's "Meet the Press."

title: Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany suffers minor injuries when his plane makes an emergency landing in a lake and he swims to safety
description: Wisconsin congressman and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tom Tiffany said he suffered minor injuries after a plane he was in made an emergency landing Saturday night on Lake Wausau in central Wiscon...
fullText:
Wisconsin congressman and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tom Tiffany said he suffered minor injuries after a plane he was in made an emergency landing Saturday night on Lake Wausau in central Wisconsin.

In a post on X, Tiffany said while returning home from the La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner, in Onalaska, Wisconsin, the plane, identified by the Federal Aviation Administration as a Beechcraft K35, lost power as it approached Wausau Downtown Airport.

The pilot made an emergency water landing in Lake Wausau, he said, and the two called 911. As the plane began to submerge, Tiffany and the pilot exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area where they waited for emergency responders, he said.

"I want to express my deepest gratitude to the pilot, the Wausau Fire Department, and all of the first responders who came to our aid so quickly," Tiffany said.

"They got us safely off the water and transported us to Aspirus Wausau Hospital, where we received excellent care."

Tiffany was released from the hospital Saturday night after receiving stitches above his right eye, he said in a post on X. The pilot was also released, he added.

"We thank God that neither of us suffered more serious injuries after the plane we were traveling in lost power," Tiffany wrote.

The Marathon County Sheriff's Office confirmed the plane experienced a mechanical issue around 8:49 p.m. while approaching the airport, according to its latest news release on Sunday. Tiffany and the pilot were rescued by a Wausau Fire Department airboat at 9:05 p.m., the sheriff's office said.

The incident is under investigation, the FAA told CNN in a statement.

The sheriff's office said the plane was marked with a buoy and asked people to stay away, according to the news release.

The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and State Patrol also responded to the scene, according to WSAW, and the investigation will be handed over to the FAA.

In dispatch audio obtained and verified by CNN, authorities mention someone inside the plane made a 911 call. Later, an official responding to the crash confirms two people inside the plane had been rescued.

"Boat heads back to landing with two victims," the official at the scene is heard telling dispatchers. "Both are alert and conscious."

"God was watching over us tonight, and I am incredibly grateful to be here in the hospital with my wife, Chris, by my side. An experience like this reminds you just how precious life is," Tiffany said in his post.

CNN has reached out to Tiffany's office, the Wisconsin DNR and State Patrol for further information.

Tiffany, a member of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, won his party's nomination for governor of Wisconsin in the primary elections, bolstered by the support of President Donald Trump.

His Democratic opponent in the governor's race, David Crowley, said in a post on X he was "grateful to God that Congressman Tiffany and no one else was hurt in this horrifying incident, which could have been a tragedy if not for the heroism of the pilot."

"I wish them and the Congressman a quick recovery and that they can find solace with their loved ones," Crowley added.

CNN's Alaa Elassar contributed to this report.

title: Can Wrexham boss Parkinson bounce back again?
description: Wrexham boss Phil Parkinson feeling the heat after sluggish start to Championship continued with thrashing at West Ham.
fullText:
The Red Dragons suffered their biggest defeat of Parkinson's tenure at the hands of the Hammers, leaving them 19th in the Championship after seven games.

With a 3-0 victory at Millwall their only win of the campaign, some have questioned whether Parkinson has taken Wrexham as far as he can.

It remains too early to draw a conclusion on that question, but in the eyes of Iwan Roberts, there was no doubt about the performance at West Ham.

He told BBC Radio Wales Sport: "It was an absolutely awful night for Wrexham, although for the first 20 to 25 minutes, they looked hard to break down.

"But once that first goal went in, there was only ever going to be one outcome. It was then a question of how many more West Ham would score."

West Ham rout among 'lowest points' for Wrexham boss

West Ham thrash Wrexham to top Championship

Latest Wrexham news, analysis and fan views

West Ham scored four times in the second half, including one less than two minutes after the restart, as Wrexham were torn apart.

"If it was a boxing match, the coach would have thrown the towel in," Roberts added.

"There was a lack of work, communication, organisation, a lack of players wanting to be brave in a difficult situation, and you can't accept that as football fans.

"If there was a measuring tape of where Wrexham are against a team who have been in the Premier League for many, many years, this was it.

"Sadly, they came up well short."

Parkinson has been under pressure before during his Wrexham tenure, and even felt the heat when the Red Dragons made a slow start to life in the second tier last season.

Wrexham won just five of their first 15 league games in 2025-26 - and drew six times - before eventually falling just short of the play-off places.

Many pointed to that inconsistent start as the reason why Wales' oldest club ultimately finished two points away from a shot at promotion.

After another summer with £30m spent in the transfer market, and two extra play-off spots up for grabs, the expectation is to go one better.

Former Wrexham midfielder Waynne Phillips does not doubt there is pressure on Parkinson, but believes the 58-year-old manager can turn things around again.

"I'm not surprised to see the reaction that comes after the game - this is how it has been for years around Wrexham," he told BBC Radio Cymru.

"I remember in the National League, if Wrexham went a game or two without winning, everyone would want Phil Parkinson out.

"But he's someone who can bounce back really well. He's been about long enough to know there will be difficult periods and difficult nights.

"I don't think Parkinson will be worrying about the noise around him, but he will worry about what he saw on Friday night."

Former Wales defender Danny Gabbidon echoed those sentiments, and believes Parkinson - the architect of so many promotions - should be afforded time.

"Pressure will start to build if those terrible results continue, but it's still very early in the season," he said on BBC Radio Wales.

"If you are slightly off it and not on your game, West Ham are capable of doing that to you. Phil Parkinson will hope it's a bad day at the office.

"Sometimes when you get those results, it wakes everybody up. Wrexham have been so good for so long now. They've charged through the divisions.

"There is no need to panic yet. We should allow the manager some time after he has been so good over the previous seasons, but you could sense his frustration after the game."

The summer signings have been a hot topic among Wrexham commentators.

While money was invested in the squad, only two players - Issa Kabore and Jacques Ekomie - have top-flight experience.

Phillips, who made over 200 appearances for Wrexham, is not convinced that some of the recruits have upgraded the side.

"It took a while last season for the new signings to settle, but up to now, I've not seen enough from the new players to believe they improve on what Wrexham had," he said.

"But one win brings another very quickly, and suddenly confidence grows. I don't for a second think that these are not good footballers.

"To come into a new club, it takes time sometimes. You're lucky if it happens from the first game.

"The goalkeeper, Anthony Patterson, has done alright, even though he conceded six goals at West Ham, so there will be questions about him.

"I haven't seen enough from Ben Whiteman in midfield to say that he's better than what they had last season.

"Callum O'Hare hardly had a kick at West Ham. There is room for them to improve, but the same is true for those who were there last season."

Wrexham will hope they can end the first block of Championship games on a high note by beating Southampton before the international break.

The Red Dragons are yet to win at home this season, and were thumped 5-1 by Saints at the Racecourse last season.

That heavy April defeat had been the only time Parkinson's Wrexham leaked five goals in a single league game since 2023, and they can ill afford a repeat.

title: Did O'Neill get team selection wrong in Old Firm defeat?
description: After a meek Premier Sports Cup exit at the hands of rivals Rangers, did Celtic boss Martin O'Neill get his team selection wrong?
fullText:
When Sebastian Tounekti's name appeared on the Celtic teamsheet for Sunday's Premier Sports Cup quarter-final, the collective groan from supporters could have drowned out the 50,000 strong Ibrox crowd.

With Yang Hyun-jun away on international duty, Tounekti made just his second start of the season in Wednesday's 1-0 win over St Johnstone, with former Hoops goalkeeper Pat Bonner describing his first-half performance in Perth as "awful".

The Tunisia winger lost possession 23 times against Simo Valakari's side - only opposition keeper Toby Steward coughed up possession more.

Tounekti toiled again at Ibrox up against Rangers right-back Dujon Sterling, so much so that he was hooked at half-time and replaced by Egypt international Haissem Hassan, who joined Celtic from Real Oviedo this summer in a deal reportedly worth up to £9m.

The substitution made little difference as Celtic slumped to a 3-0 defeat, having been one down at the break.

"That was a question, should Tounekti start or not?" Bonner said.

"O'Neill went with him but I think I think he now realises that maybe he's not the player that's going to be dominant in this team.

"Sterling absolutely dominated him, and Sterling was playing almost like a third centre-half.

"Out of all of the wingers we've seen, I think Hassan should have started. He's maybe not 100 per cent match fit but you pay big money for these guys they have to perform."

'McInnes delivers togetherness & intensity in Old Firm gobsmacker'

Rangers overwhelm meek Celtic to clinch semi-final spot

Rangers v Aberdeen & Edinburgh derby in League Cup semis

Tounekti's spot in Celtic's front three was not the only attacking quandary for O'Neill going into the game.

Camilo Duran had excelled through the middle while Kasper Hogh - another big-money summer signing - was out injured.

But with Hogh fit again, the Dane started at McDiarmid Park and led the line again at Ibrox, with Duran moved out wide.

Both struggled to make an impact and former Rangers man Andy Halliday was scathing in his assessment of Hogh's performance.

"Kasper Hogh has blown hot and cold for Celtic so far, but he was absolutely freezing today," Halliday said on Premier Sports.

"On the ball, off the ball - no desire, no willingness to get back and defend for his team."

After Hogh was brought off on 64 minutes, Duran was deployed through the middle, only to be substituted himself 13 minutes later for Shim Mheuka.

O'Neill also opted to break up the centre-back pairing of Cameron Carter-Vickers and Auston Trusty that had started seven of Celtic's nine games this season. Kieran Tierney returned at left-back and Liam Scales shifted inside to partner Carter-Vickers.

On-loan Wolves goalkeeper Sam Johstone, who also started at St Johnstone, was perhaps a surprise inclusion given Viljami Sinisalo has kept four clean sheets in his eight appearances this season.

Despite some sharp saves in Perth, the 33-year-old looked rusty at Ibrox, maybe unsurprising given it was just his second competitive appearance since March.

Rangers striker Kevin Kelsy should have scored when Johnstone's clearance went straight to him early on and Kim Min-Su had an effort cleared off the line by Scales after the four-time England international palmed a cross into his path.

Johnstone spent the rest of the game being goaded by Rangers supporters every time he was on the ball.

"If you've been beaten in a game you always think about selection," manager O'Neill said post-match.

"I'll think about my own part in proceedings first of all and then we'll see. I wanted people to experience this atmosphere and they certainly did that today."

Gordy: Martin O'Neill and Shaun Maloney got team selection and formation totally wrong. It was obvious Rangers would overload the midfield and fight for the second ball, physically and mentally we were not up to the task. Colby Donovan, Mika Baur and especially Sebastian Tounekti were not up to the standard needed to play for us.

Moe: Team selection was wrong, Viljami Sinisalo should have played he had the experience already.

Phillip: Worst performance in five years, a mess from the get go starting with leaving Hassan out. Johnstone a disaster in goal, Sinisalo needs to go back in. A good look in the mirror needed and midfield signings in January.

Willie: Shocking team selection from the start.

Biggar: Martin O'Neill got two big team selection decisions wrong. Tounekti shouldn't be anywhere near the Celtic first team. Hassan should've started on the right, with Duran on the left. Sinisalo should've been back in goal, very harsh on him to lose his starting place.

title: Foden sees red as Mainoo impresses - Manchester derby ratings
description: How Manchester United and Manchester City players rated in the derby clash at Old Trafford.
fullText:
Phil Foden's first-half red card did not prevent Manchester City extending their perfect start to the season by beating Manchester United at Old Trafford.

Here's how Simon Stone rated the United players and Shamoon Hafez scored City's.

What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean?

Senne Lammens: Not as busy as he might have expected to be. Absolutely vital save from Fernandez to prevent City second. 7

Diogo Dalot: If only he had been able to control Bruno Fernandes' chipped pass into the penalty area he might have marked his 250th Manchester United appearance with a rare goal. Didn't look down the line to see he was clearly offside as United pressed just before half-time. Screwed shot wide after break. 4

Harry Maguire: Decent performance from veteran central defender and not far away from an equaliser with late header. Needless push on Enzo Fernandez in the box, for which he was booked. 6

Lisandro Martinez: Didn't dive in when Bruno Fernandes played a pass towards his own goal straight to Erling Haaland and won the ball from the Norwegian. Decent effort 7

Patrick Dorgu: Replaced Luke Shaw at left back in the starting 11 and did OK but doesn't have the same link with Rashford. Attempted block proved so crucial to City's opener. 6

Kobbie Mainoo: Another assured display in front of England boss Thomas Tuchel. Came close to giving his side the lead just after half-time and was home side's most effective midfielder. 8

Youri Tielemans (off 66, Sesko): Best performance of the season so far but yet to make the standout contribution expected. 7

Bryan Mbeumo: Probably United's most-effective attacking player. Header just wide before injury-time effort saved. 8

Bruno Fernandes: Fortunate to get away with no sanction at all over the incident that led to Foden's dismissal. Not one of his better efforts 6

Marcus Rashford (off 83, Zirkzee): Curling long-range free-kick against the post with Donnarumma beaten and shot into side-netting but still waiting for first goal since his return. 6

Matheus Cunha: Preferred to Benjamin Sesko in starting line-up and dragged early shot wide. Got involved on plenty of occasions, but again by dropping deep. Off target with a second-half opportunity. 7

Benjamin Sesko (on 66, Tielemans): Brought on to make an impact and tried his luck from distance soon afterwards. 6

Joshua Zirkzee (on 83, Rashford) 6

Subs not used: Darlow, Mazraoui, Mount, Yoro, Santos, Heaven, Lacey.

Gianluigi Donnarumma: Saw his post hit twice but made a good stop to deny Fernandes from range and a sensational one in injury-time from Mbeumo for the clean sheet. 8

Matheus Nunes: Overcome his nightmare performance here from April 2025. Showed some neat touches and generally shackled Rashford well. 7

Ruben Dias: The Portuguese has stepped up to take on the responsibility of being captain and was solid at the back once again. 7

Marc Guehi: Beginning to form an impressive partnership with his skipper and needed to be sturdy after City were reduced to 10 men. 7

Josko Gvardiol: Looks like left-back is where his position will be in this team. Handled Mbeumo brilliantly throughout and provided the cross for Haaland's goal. 8

Elliot Anderson: Busy and hard working in the centre of the park, as is now expected. Managed more touches of the ball than any City team-mate. 7

Enzo Fernandez: Given licence to roam and has fitted in seamlessly into midfield. The Argentine made an excellent challenge to thwart Tielemans and struck the post in the second half. 8

Antoine Semenyo: Has struggled in recent games and was wasteful once more. Place in the starting XI could come under pressure from Iliman Ndiaye. 5

Phil Foden: Total head loss in the cauldron of the derby. Given a straight red after kicking Fernandes in the stomach on 23 minutes and fortunate not to cost his side. 3

Rayan Cherki: Created very little after being move to the right. Not helped by a fellow attacking player getting himself sent off before being taken off at half-time. 5

Erling Haaland: On the periphery of the game in the first half, the fewest touches of any player. But came alive to open the scoring in with a cool, first-time finish in front of his own fans. 7

Iliman Ndiaye (on 45, Cherki): Caused some concern to the United backline with his direct running. 6

Nico O'Reilly (on 81, Fernandez) 6

Subs not used: Rulli, Kovacic, Reis, Bouaddi, Allan, Khusanov, Lewis.
