title: The tournament Jannik Sinner is aiming to return at is revealed in new injury update after missing the US Open
description: The 2026 US Open unfolded without the world’s best tennis player, Jannik Sinner, in action. Sinner, who was denied in last year’s final at Flushing...
fullText:
The 2026 US Open unfolded without the world's best tennis player, Jannik Sinner, in action.

Sinner, who was denied in last year's final at Flushing Meadows by Carlos Alcaraz, has been sidelined since his Wimbledon triumph with a knee injury.

The setback saw the world number one withdraw from the Canadian Open, the Cincinnati Open and ultimately the US Open.

In Sinner's absence, his rival Alcaraz made his long-awaited return to tennis after four months out and reached the quarterfinals in New York before being beaten by Ben Shelton.

With Alcaraz officially back and healthy again, it won't be long before Sinner makes his comeback to the ATP Tour.

According to Sky Sports Italy, Sinner underwent a three-week course of treatment at J Medical in Turin for extra-articular tendon inflammation.

Everything reportedly went well, and Sinner is now due to head back to his main residence in Monte-Carlo.

Sinner is set to resume training and is looking to finally return to professional tennis at the China Open in Beijing, which starts on the 30th of September.

He is the defending champion at the ATP 500 event, having comfortably beaten Learner Tien in the final last year.

Sinner also captured the China Open title in 2023 and finished as the runner-up in 2024 after delivering a thrilling final against eventual champion Alcaraz.

Sinner will not be taking part in the Laver Cup in London, which gets underway on the 25th of September.

Both Alcaraz and Sinner's time out has presented a golden opportunity for several stars to do well at big tournaments.

Taylor Fritz was the first player to take advantage of their absence, with the US number two clinching the Washington Open title at the start of the North American hard-court swing.

His compatriot, Shelton, then followed suit at the Canadian Open, where he defended the title to win his second ATP Masters 1000 crown.

The Cincinnati Open was won by 22-year-old Arthur Fils, who put together an impressive run to hoist his first Masters trophy.

The US Open will mark the second Grand Slam this year not won by Sinner or Alcaraz, with Shelton and Alexander Zverev set to battle it out for the title.

title: Three Things Learned from UNC-ETSU
description: Carolina’s given up 13 points in 8 quarters of football in 2026.
fullText:
Carolina loves to play in the rain, apparently. In two rain-soaked games so far, the Tar Heels are now 2-0, with the defense allowing 13 points across eight quarters of play. The game against TCU in Dublin, a sloppy affair in which the team that made the fewest mistakes left with the crystal trophy, demonstrated UNC could win that sort of game. Jelani Thurman emerged as a primary playmaker in the passing game. The defense, spearheaded by a breakout from Xavier Lewis (THB's player of that game) showed some teeth on the money downs lacking in last season's defense.

Games against FCS opponents don't often provide much insight. After defeating the East Tennessee State University Buccaneers 35-3, the Tar Heels prepare to head to Clemson next Saturday. What might we have learned from the game against ETSU?

Perhaps the biggest surprise from the game was UNC only scoring 35 points and posting 427 yards on a team that surrendered 49 points and 514 yards to the Campbell Camels last week. However, that was less an issue of the offense being ineffective than the offense simply not getting many possessions. UNC averaged eight yards a play but only ran 53 offensive plans on the day. Fourth quarter stats with the second string offense and conservative play calling lowered that number.

ETSU, meanwhile, ran 67 plays. FCS rent-a-wins don't usually produce a stat line in which the renter runs 14 less plays than the rentee. In the first half, ETSU controlled the ball for 20 minutes to UNC's 10. Part of that was the offense scoring quickly, but the other part was the defense surrendering long drives that let ETSU nibble the edges with quick passing. ETSU then converted third downs by running up the middle on a defense spread out horizontally. ETSU went 5-10 on third down in the first half and got deep into UNC territory on its third drive before a holding penalty took a touchdown off the board. A facemask penalty on the next play pushed the Bucs even further back, and the field goal attempt produced a doink.

The "bend but don't break, then unleash the pass rush when the defense forces a third and long" approach last season failed largely because the defense didn't produce on third and fourth downs. It has been a winner thus far this season, at least where it most counts (points allowed), with UNC giving up only 13 points in the first two games. That's excellent. The price, however, is an offense that has to be efficient with its limited opportunities.

Between TCU and ETSU, UNC's opponents have held the ball almost 14 minutes more than the Tar Heels. Put another way, the defense has been on the field almost an entire quarter more the offense over two games. This year, the offense can't be blamed for it.

Sadler's elite athleticism in high school produced eye-popping stats on both sides of the ball and earned him player of the year honors in Michigan. Would Bobby Petrino and Bill Belichick trust a true freshman to play a significant role on offense? After Saturday's game, the answer appears to be yes.

Sadler split snaps with Kekahuna evenly against TCU, although in that tight contest he was only targeted two times. Yesterday, Petrino clearly made an effort to get Sadler the ball as well. On the game's opening play, Edwards locked on the speedster and underthrew a ball Sadler still should have caught. (Sidenote: Jordan Shipp was wide open and likely walks into the end zone with an on-target throw). Sadler's 66 receiving yards all came when the game remained a contest, and his four targets tied with Thurman for the team lead. The offense wants Sadler to be a weapon to complement Thurman and Shipp, and today Sadler demonstrated that potential.

A passing game that features those three could be dangerous. However, that will require the offense to average more than the 55 snaps per game it's averaging so far this season.

Melkart Abou Jaoude proved himself last season and entered this season for UNC with pre-season All ACC honors. Two weeks ago against TCU, former walk-on Xavier Lewis owned the TCU offensive line, generating havoc left and right on his way to seven tackles, two sacks, and four-and-a-half tackles for loss. Today's defensive line spotlight went to Jaylen Harvey.

With Melkart Abou Jaoude sitting out the game with a hand injury, UNC needed someone to step up as that edge presence, and Harvey delivered. UNC's first turnover of the season, an interception by Greg Smith, came after Harvey beat his block and quickly got into the face of ETSU QB Mason Mims, forcing the ball out and setting up Smith to make a play. Harvey followed that effort with two more sacks in the first half before exiting the game with what appeared to be a mild ankle injury.

If Harvey can be similarly effective against P4 opponents, that gives the Tar Heels three guys with proven ability to disrupt an offensive backfield.

In an ideal world, UNC would have raced out to a big lead, giving its offensive depth some badly needed reps. That largely didn't happen. Miles O'Neill added six pass attempts to bring his college total to 26. At 3.7 yards per attempt, the throws were safe. True freshman Cristian Alvarez earned a lot of snaps at right guard and seemed to acquit himself well. Demon June, who didn't see much action against TCU until the game's final drive, notched three touchdowns when his teammates got the ball into the deep red zone. Perhaps he's earning the nickname, "The Finisher." However, June entered the season with many assuming he'd be the feature back in the offense.

UNC now sets its sights on Clemson, and it would be fair to assume some of this week's preparation in part laid a foundation for that game. Will Clemson try to mimic some of ETSU's offensive game plan and hope for better results with superior athletes? Will UNC try to emulate LSU's defensive dominance up front with Melkart, Xavier, and Jaylen? Next Saturday offers Bill Belichick a real opportunity to open the season 3-0, something few thought possible three weeks ago.

title: Henry Cejudo: Tom Aspinall ‘needs to vacate or be stripped at this point’
description: Henry Cejudo wants to see a new UFC heavyweight champion
fullText:
Henry Cejudo has had enough of Tom Aspinall sitting on the sidelines.

Aspinall has been out of action since October 2025, when he suffered a pair of eye pokes from Ciryl Gane in the main event of UFC 321 that left him unable to continue and rendered the heavyweight title fight a no-contest. Since then, Aspinall has been in full recovery mode, undergoing eye surgery and steadily healing, with no timetable for his comeback established as of yet.

Next month will mark a full year off for Aspinall, so Cejudo thinks he and the UFC need to get on the same page when it comes to putting his belt up for grabs.

"I think Tom Aspinall needs to vacate or be stripped at this point," Cejudo said on his Pound-4-Pound podcast. "What I'm saying is, as a champion, if you're hurt and you're unwilling to compete, vacate the belt, let somebody be called undisputed until you're actually back."

It's been a slow climb to the top for Aspinall, who has competed just four times since July 2022. On that date, Aspinall suffered a freak knee injury in a loss to Curtis Blaydes that shelved him for a year, and though he later went on to capture and defend an interim heavyweight title—including avenging his loss to Blaydes—much of the past few years were wasted in a fruitless attempt to book a matchup with undisputed heavyweight champion Jon Jones.

Eventually, Jones retired, and Aspinall was elevated to undisputed status. However, his first title defense ended in disaster when Gane's foul brought an unceremonious end to their duel. Aspinall is currently employing Matchroom Boxing boss Eddie Hearn as a manager, putting him in an awkward place as Hearn and UFC CEO Dana White continue to publicly butt heads over several topics, including Hearn calling Aspinall's UFC contract "a f*cking disgrace."

"Eddie Hearn does not help Tom Aspinall," Cejudo said. "He's got no leverage. Time's almost up. It's f*cking Oct. 25, by the time Oct. 26 hits, he has a right to be stripped after that. Eddie Hearn cannot help him if Tom Aspinall does not fight; it's just not there. There's no negotiations, especially you're poking the bear.

"Dana White's the bear. Dana White's the f*cking pink elephant in the room. You're f*cking with the boss. If you're doing that, it's not good business to have Dana White as your enemy."

Though several UFC champions have gone a year without fighting and retained their titles—including current bantamweight champion Kayla Harrison—Cejudo doubts the UFC will wait much longer for Aspinall to make his way back into the octagon.

"Once that year is up, you're done," Cejudo said. "You're getting stripped, or they're telling you, 'Hey, you're getting stripped, or you're going to vacate. Which one do you want to do? Do you want to strip, or do you want to vacate and come out with your words, where you could do it and it sounds a little better?'

"But f*ck no, you're getting stripped."

title: Has Aaron Nola Been Unlucky with the Homer Thing?
description: Moonshot misfortune? Longball luck? Or just cold tater truth?
fullText:
It's been a good season for Aaron Nola. Especially in the second half, he's looked solid and reliable; a comforting return to form, like a rerun of a favorite TV show. There is one thing that's still plagued him, though, a thorn that he can't quite pull out of his paw: the homers. The home run has seemed like an almost ubiquitous part of the Nola start. His 34 gopher balls surrendered are the most league-wide, tied with Jeffrey Springs, and one ahead of Shota Imanaga. The homer problem (the downtowner dilemma, the tater trouble, the four-bagger fretting), has gone on for far too long to be dismissed as happenstance. It is, unfortunately, as real as the Phanatic's green fur. Case in point: I drafted this article on Friday afternoon, just prior to Nola's start, hoping I wouldn't have to rewrite any of it; it is now Saturday evening and I am rewriting it to account for the two homers he surrendered. That being said, what if he's been at least a little unlucky?

Nola has allowed 34 homers this season, but per Statcast's numbers, his expected number of homers allowed is 27.3 (that's with the adjusted model, which accounts for environmental variables, and which we'll use elsewhere in this article; it's 30.4 if you're accounting for trajectory only). That puts him at 6.7 homers above expected in 2026, second-most league-wide. Even if his actual homer total was identical to the expected, he'd still be one of the most-homer prone pitchers in baseball this season; he'd just rank fourth instead of first. Still, that might suggest that the homer problem isn't quite as bad as it's seemed in 2026.

Then again, if you look at the one pitcher who has a a greater gap between his actual homers surrendered and expected homers surrendered, it's Springs, who's allowed the same number of actual homers as Nola. And the pitcher who's got the third-biggest gap in that regard is Imanaga. That stands to reason: the more prone you are to surrendering the sort of long ball that can become a homer, the more prone you'll be to surrendering the sort of borderline ball that might become a homer and might not become one, with the vagaries of ballpark design and environment determining its fate. So while we can say that Nola's been a little unlucky, homer-wise, I don't think it'd be quite right to suggest that the gap between his expected and actual homer stats is purely or even primarily the result of misfortune. He really does have a genuine homer issue.

(It's perhaps worth noting here that of all the pitchers who have allowed at least 20 dingers this season, Nola has the lowest percentage, 2o.6, of what Statcast refers to as No Doubters— homers that would be homers no matter which ballpark they're born in. Compare to Imanaga's 29.4%, or Springs' 42.4%. I'm not convinced that it's a terribly meaningful fact, but I do find it curious).

That being said, there is one way in which Nola is arguably unlucky: he plays half his games at the third homer-happiest park in baseball, per Park Factors, and the one most prone to allowing homers to the lefties who already have the platoon advantage over him. It's not just the dimensions of CBP, either: per Statcast, Citizens Bank Park ranks ninth among MLB ballparks for extra distance added to balls by the effects of the weather, environment, etc.

I say this is arguably unlucky because this wasn't really luck; he chose to resign with the team that calls Citizens Bank Park home. Then again, I suppose you could argue that luck was involved given that he had no say in where he was drafted, which eventually set up the sequence of events that led to him choosing to resign with the incumbent club. But that's getting awfully philosophical. Speaking of philosophical, let's imagine some hypotheticals.

Imagine an alternate world in which Nola pitches every one of his starts in Boston (perhaps a dystopian future in which only Boston remains, perhaps a world in which some sort of New England envy results in every ballclub directly copying the dimensions and environment of famed Fenway, it doesn't matter). That hypothetical Boston Nola would have allowed only 15 homers this year. Now imagine if only Philadelphia existed. Most people, we can all agree, would be happier in such a world. But Aaron Nola would not: he'd have allowed 35 homers in this alternate All-Philly 2026, one more than he actually has. And that is the only park that would produce such an effect: place all his starts in any other ballpark, and he allows fewer gopher balls than the real Nola has. Citizens Bank Park is a wonderful place for everyone, except for Braves fans, Mets fans, and homer-prone pitchers.

As an example: take this homer Jake Burger hit against Nola in his first start of the season:

That's obviously an unlucky break for Nola: just a few inches to the left and it would be foul, with no harm done other than some induced heartburn. But it's even more unlucky than it appears: if it had been hit in any other ballpark in baseball, it wouldn't have been a home run (although that's by Statcast's environment-adjusted model; per the trajectory-only model it would've been a dinger in 17 of 30 parks).

And this one, hit by Francisco Alvarez back in July, was even more unlucky for Nola.

It barely cleared the wall at CBP, and it wouldn't have been gone at any other park. Even if we use the trajectory-only model, it still would've been gone in only two other parks.

But the most unlucky homer of all was probably this one, hit by Luke Keaschall at the Field of Dreams game:

If that game was played at any standard big league ballpark, that ball stays in the yard rather than finding a happy home in the corn.

Any pitcher in the league, of course, has similar stories, of homers that would've ended as harmless fly balls if the location had been different, or if it had been a few degrees cooler, or if the wind hadn't been blowing in quite that direction. Betteridge's Law of Headlines applies here: Nola's homer problem isn't the result of bad luck. Misfortune may have resulted in it looking slightly worse than it really is, but the underlying problem is real. But so is Nola's return to form this season, and what he's done for the 2026 Phils. We ought to feel lucky to have him.

title: 2 Cowboys to buy, 2 to sell versus the Giants
description: Which 2 Cowboys do you think will have huge games?
fullText:
The Dallas Cowboys versus the New York Giants and an intra-division game that will set the tone for the start of the season. The Cowboys will need to play to their strengths, and limit their weaknesses to keep the good vibes going from the offseason.

Here are two plyers who should excel in this game, and two who may have a struggle on their hands.

How could this list start with anybody else? Prescott has played an entire season's worth of games against the Giants in his career. In those 17 games, Prescott has a passer rating of 101.5 with 4,346 yards, 31 touchdowns and 9 interceptions. Prescott is 14-3 against the Giants in his career and, at one point, before getting pulled early last year against New York in Week 18, had won 14 straight games against his divisional foe.

14 wins spanning various coaching staffs, new players and new front offices, Prescott has beaten them all, so even with a lot of new faces in the Meadowlands this year, look for Prescott's dominance to continue as he continues to helm one of the league's best offenses.

This isn't as much an indictment of Overshown's ability as it is an understanding of what the Giants and some of their players can bring to the table. Last season, the Cowboys linebacker struggled mightily in space, against every team, really. Now with Jaxson Dart as the starter, be prepared for the Cowboys' linebackers to be put in frequent conflict with Dart's ability to scramble.

Overshown, recovering from another knee injury, will have to show he can hold his own against the likes of Dart, Cam Skattebo, Isiah Likely, and all the receivers the Giants will flood the middle of the defense with.

The Giants had one of the worst run defenses last season, ranking 31 out of 32 teams in the league. In 2026, even with a lot of players added to this defense, the most notable departure was New York sending DT Dexter Lawrence to Cincinnati.

Williams averaged 5.4 yards per carry last year in 18 carries against this team. Even without Tyler Smith at LG, look for a healthy number of carries for Williams and for the second-year Cowboy to continue his efficiency against a shaky interior defensive line.

Terence Steele's struggles last season are nothing new to Cowboys fans. As it stands, he is going to be the Week 1 starter at RT. What is new is that the RT situation has deteriorated to the point where the Cowboys felt it necessary to bring in another struggling tackle, Broderick Jones, to compete for the job. A more ominous indictment of a positional assessment might not currently exist in the NFL.

Steele will have to face the likes of Abdul Carter, Brian Burns and Kavon Thibodeaux- not an inspiring trial by fire. Even so, if Dak and the offense manage his liability, they could overcome the deficiencies at that position.

title: John McEnroe claims there’s a ‘strong possibility’ Novak Djokovic will retire in 2027
description: Novak Djokovic’s absence throughout almost the entirety of this US Open has been eerie. It is not a situation we have become accustomed to. However,...
fullText:
Novak Djokovic's absence throughout almost the entirety of this US Open has been eerie. It is not a situation we have become accustomed to.

However, at 39 years of age, perhaps it is time we start expecting shock early exits from a player now competing with people over half his age.

What he has achieved and continues to achieve is legendary beyond belief, and his eventual retirement will rock the sporting world as nothing we have ever seen before.

And now, speaking at a Eurosport and HBO event ahead of the men's US Open final, John McEnroe thinks he knows when the Serbian might call time on his supreme career.

He began with an assessment of Novak Djokovic's year, reviewing the exceptional highs and the more recent crushing lows.

McEnroe admitted: "On the one hand, one thinks that age is taking its toll, as happens to all athletes at some point. On the other hand, he has had an incredible streak.

"He beat Jannik Sinner in Australia, reached the final and won the first set against Carlos Alcaraz and played well. Then he reached the semifinals of Wimbledon, and got a big victory over Felix Auger-Aliassime in the previous round. That made me think that, when I got to the US Open, he was probably the third or fourth best player in the world.

"So what we saw in the first round was shocking. As they say, time is invincible."

McEnroe was then asked whether he felt Djokovic might retire in 2027, following a tough end to his Grand Slam season.

The American pundit theorised: "Well, you would certainly think so. He's 39 for starters, you know, when it's just way past most people's expiration date and tennis, including mine.

"You don't want to get to a point and say, 'Why did I stop when maybe I could have won more. That's sort of what Novak's facing. You got to the finals of Australia. He's like, maybe I could win one more.

"Will he stop next year? It seems like it's gonna be soon. You would think that's a strong possibility, but we'll have to wait and see."

If the 24-time Grand Slam champion were to retire next year, it would go against plenty of his prior comments about the subject.

However, this was before Djokovic revealed he was dealing with a health issue that has persisted for some time, and certainly impacted him during his first-round exit at the US Open.

Despite this, whenever asked, he has always insisted that the 2028 LA Olympics remain his ultimate final goal for retirement.

He has claimed: "The only thing that I have in my head, which gives me motivation, is the Olympics of 2028 in Los Angeles.

"It is the only thing that at this moment, professionally speaking, I have in my vision at this point.

"And playing for the national team and Grand Slams. But not even the Grand Slams, not as much as the Olympics."

And, more recently in his documentary, Djokovic said: "Why would I talk about retirement when I still keep proving to myself that I can still win?"

Djokovic admitted his retirement has felt closer than ever earlier this year. Perhaps, sadly, McEnroe might be on to something.

title: Sean Payton will have 'some suggestions' and 'some mandates' for Davis Webb
description: Sean Payton says he has a healthy dynamic with new OC/play-caller Davis Webb, but he admitted some plays will be "mandates" instead of suggestions.
fullText:
When the Denver Broncos face the Kansas City Chiefs on Monday Night Football in Week 1, it will mark the regular-season debut of new offensive coordinator and play-caller Davis Webb.

Broncos head coach Sean Payton, who has handled play-calling duties for most of his career, promoted Webb from quarterbacks coach to OC this offseason, handing over the play-calling role in the process.

Payton is an extremely hands-on coach, and he takes pride in his offense — and his perfect plays. So it will be fascinating to see if Webb has any level of a hot seat in 2026. If things don't go well initially, will Payton take back play-calling? If Payton doesn't like a call in Week 1, will he overrule Webb?

Earlier this summer, Payton was asked if he'll make suggestions to Webb.

"Yes," Payton said. "Some suggestions, some mandates. It'll work fine."

Payton said "mandates" with a smile, and he has said he'll have a "healthy" dynamic with Webb on the sideline.

As for Webb, he's not worried about the possibility of Payton looking over his shoulder. In fact, he's eager to learn from one of the game's best.

"[T]hat was one reason why I wanted to be here was with Sean here," Webb said. "I trust him; he trusts me. We think very similar. I know how he wants the game to be played. It's the same offense for the most part, just little tweaks here and there, but this is a Sean Payton-coached football team, a Sean Payton offensive philosophy, and we're just going to grow ... The most attractive thing was leaning on Sean, being in game plan meetings with him, using his experience. I think that's going to benefit a young play caller."

Payton and Webb appear to have a great relationship and a good plan for their game-day dymanic going into the season. We'll see how it holds up once the games begin.

title: Fresno, we have a quarterback
description: No, it wasn’t against a top ranked defense. And no, it wasn’t against a P4 conference opponent. Nonetheless, Jayden Mandal put some doubts to rest on Saturday night about him being capable enough to be Fresno State’s starting quarterback. Mandal went 23-for-26 for 316 yards and two touchdowns, and a rushing touchdown, in the Bulldogs’ […]
fullText:
No, it wasn't against a top ranked defense. And no, it wasn't against a P4 conference opponent. Nonetheless, Jayden Mandal put some doubts to rest on Saturday night about him being capable enough to be Fresno State's starting quarterback.

Mandal went 23-for-26 for 316 yards and two touchdowns, and a rushing touchdown, in the Bulldogs' 49-3 victory over Sacramento State. A stark contrast from his opening week performance against USC, where Mandal was 7-for-15 for 77 yards and an interception.

The junior gunslinger was responsible for the first three touchdowns for the Bulldogs, all of which came in the second quarter.

Mandal first found Speedy Luke for an 18-yard touchdown. He then followed that up with a 73-yard connection to Ezekiel Avit for another score, before using his legs on a quarterback sneak from 1-yard out to make it 22-0 Fresno State.

"I'm really excited for the young man," head coach Matt Entz said following the contest. "He had some people make plays for him. And he did a really good job of orchestrating the offense."

After a rough first outing against the Trojans, many fans and "pundits" wanted to see Fresno State's second-string quarterback getting some reps. Aside from Mandal's numbers, he was also responsible for a few of USC's points as he was sacked twice for safety in the loss.

However, Entz stayed the course with Mandal, stating that it was inexperience for Mandal and that a change now would cause him to lose the team. That vote of confidence for Mandal and his talent paid off for the Bulldogs on Saturday night. And now with the offense relying on both the pass and run games, the Dawgs have a shot to turn things around and perhaps become a contender for the College Football Playoff.

Mandal will now lead Fresno State into San Jose next Saturday night to clash with the rival Spartans for the Valley Trophy. That game is at 8 p.m. Pacific Time and will be on Fox Sports 1.

title: Boks power & All Blacks of old - what did we learn from series?
description: What did we learn from South Africa's Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series victory over New Zealand?
fullText:
South Africa further cemented themselves as the world's best team with a 3-1 victory over New Zealand in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.

After losing the opening Test in Johannesburg, the world champions won three straight games, comfortably claiming the series with a 43-28 win in Baltimore.

The fourth Test, played in the United States, came after three Tests in South Africa where the All Blacks continued to show promising signs under Dave Rennie.

With the Rugby World Cup next year, what did we learn from the series, which replaced this year's Rugby Championship and will be played again in 2029?

New Zealander Tony Brown's arrival as attack coach in 2024 pointed to South Africa's ambition to dominate in all facets of the game.

The former Highlanders head coach, who will join the All Blacks in 2028, is known for creating a cohesive attacking shape built on sharp ball movement.

But having been outscored in terms of tries over the first two Tests, the Springboks flipped their pack-power trump card - pivotal to their back-to-back World Cup successes - to prevent a repeat of New Zealand's victorious 1996 series win in South Africa.

Nothing illustrated that more than a monster maul that started just inside New Zealand's 22 and ended with Malcolm Marx peeling off to score the decisive try under the posts.

That came after a penalty try from a scrum in the first half. In Baltimore, their power again proved too much.

"South Africa have tried to play expansively a couple of times when we have dominance after hurting teams in the maul or scrum," Schalk Brits, a 2019 World Cup winner, told BBC Sport.

"New Zealand didn't have that dominance in the forwards, but people said they played beautiful rugby. I don't care if it is beautiful or not.

"Beauty is in the eye of the beholder and I love a maul and scrum."

Fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, who was injured at the end of May, returned to start all four Tests. He was initially named on the bench for the second match, only for Handre Pollard to withdraw.

Despite improving as the series went on, the 24-year-old lacked his usual flashes of individual brilliance.

It remains to be seen whether South Africa turn back to 32-year-old Pollard, as they did in 2023, on the biggest occasions to close out games.

Rassie Erasmus' experienced back-to-back World Cup winners - Marx (32), Eben Etzebeth (34), Pieter-Steph du Toit (34), Siya Kolisi (35), Damian de Allende (34), Cheslin Kolbe (32) - all remain regular starters.

The world champions have proven they can also play an exciting brand of attacking rugby, but appeasing the masses will not matter if a familiar formula can bring them three straight World Cups.

Scott Robertson's dismissal in January after two years as head coach sunk New Zealand to a new low.

Rennie, not the flashiest appointment, had to hit the ground running, and a stunning Test win over South Africa at Ellis Park was a case of doing just that.

The 33-16 victory injected jeopardy into a series which many had the Springboks winning comfortably, given their home advantage and recent dominance.

Hurricanes half-backs Cam Roigard and Ruben Love, both aged 25, were trusted by Rennie to instil a return to the All Blacks way - the ability to score from transition from anywhere on the field and compound scoreboard pressure.

Four or more tries in each Test in South Africa showed just that, with the third Test all square at half-time.

"Scott Robertson was a good culture coach but maybe not a brilliant technical coach. Dave Rennie is a brilliant technical coach," former England wing Ugo Monye told Rugby Union Weekly.

"After the Nations Championship, you could see the structures and how they want to play. I think the All Blacks' backline is the most skilled in World Rugby."

Love struggled to have the same commanding impact in Tests two and three, with fly-half Richie Mo'unga returning for the Baltimore game, his first Test since the World Cup final.

The 32-year-old Mo'unga, who is back after a stint in Japan, was not at the standard that made him one of the best fly-halves at the 2023 World Cup.

However, getting him back up to speed will be an All Blacks goal over the next 12 months.

Former England scrum-half Danny Care said: "Imagine what New Zealand would do with a platform and some dominance. It is great for the game that they are coming back to be the All Blacks of old, and the next 12 months will be fascinating."

South Africa live for must-win games. That is when, according to Brits, the Boks "come alive".

Defeat at Ellis Park cost them their world number one status - which was quickly regained - but also exposed a vulnerability.

South Africa, who lost matches in the pool stages of the past two World Cups, are currently the favourites to win next year's tournament in Australia, bringing a pressure they have not experienced previously.

"We hate being the favourite, we almost have to have our backs against the wall," Brits said.

"We prefer not to have the eyes on us and move under the radar. I think that is the best way for any team."

Back-to-back Six Nations champions France sent a weakened side to Christchurch in July and lost 34-32 to New Zealand.

When matched against the Springboks last November, France were beaten emphatically, 32-17.

Brits believes France are "the most settled" and offer tactical flexibility similar to that of the world champions.

"I feel like South Africa have an advantage as they can play multiple styles, and it feels like most other nations don't have that capability," Brits said.

"The only team that can play multiple styles is France, as they can grind it out with the forwards, play the kicking game and the expansive game as well."

He added that England still need to become what they are "supposed to be" and to keep an eye on Ireland, who are travelling "under the radar" after peaking in previous World Cup cycles prior to the tournament.

"Ireland still have amazing rugby players and coaches – the best coaches out there - and a top-four squad," Brits added. "Be careful of Ireland."

title: Rangers beat Celtic 3-0 in the first Old Firm derby of the season
description: Celtic fans were barred from the game following a Scottish league review of the disorder that marred the Scottish Cup quarterfinal match between the teams in March.  The match also marked Rangers’ first victory over Celtic under new coach Derek McInnes.
fullText:
GLASGOW, Scotland (AP) — Dan Neil scored a double and Rangers beat Celtic 3-0 in the first Old Firm derby of the season Sunday — in the Scottish league cup quarterfinals.

Celtic fans were barred from the game following a Scottish league review of the disorder that marred the Scottish Cup quarterfinal match between the teams in March.

There were no immediate reports of disorder from the latest encounter.

The match also marked Rangers' first victory over Celtic under new coach Derek McInnes.

Neil, who wore the captain's armband, put Rangers ahead from the edge of the area midway through the first half.

Newly signed Kevin Kelsy scored Rangers' second and Neil added a third with another fine finish in the 75th.

It was the first domestic defeat this season for Celtic, which was also eliminated from the Champions League qualifying playoffs by Austrian club LASK.

In the Oct. 31-Nov. 1 semifinals, Rangers will face Aberdeen, while Hearts will play Hibernian.

The final is scheduled for Dec. 13.

Rangers will visit Celtic next Sunday as the teams meet again in the Scottish Premier League.

title: Ohio State has to wake up from this big-game ‘Groundhog Day’
description: According to director Harold Ramis, Phil Connors lived the same day 12,400 times in “Groundhog Day.”Hopefully Ryan Day can break out of his big-game time loop before it gets that far.
fullText:
In life, I think that it is exceedingly healthy to turn every stumble, every setback, every failure into an opportunity to learn and grow. After all, once it's over, those negatives are in the past, and there's nothing you can do about them. But at some point, if the same stumbles, setbacks, and failures keep happening over and over again, you have to start wondering whether the lesson is actually being learned.

Stop me if you've heard this one before, but last night the Ohio State Buckeyes got out to a commanding lead, and instead of continuing the aggressive game plan that put them in that position, they went ultra-conservative, hoping to run out the clock and preserve the victory. From there, the lack of creativity and intensity allowed OSU's opponent to get back into the game. Ohio State's special teams faltered when they needed them most; the offense couldn't extend drives, meaning that the defense was on the field for an inordinate amount of time and eventually looked like a shell of what it had earlier in the game; OSU squandered trips into the red zone; they quit going to the playmakers that got them that lead; there were inexplicable clock and game management blunders; and eventually all hell broke loose. Sometimes, by sheer force of talent, the Buckeyes overcome this insanity and still hold on to win… but sometimes they don't.

We've seen versions of this very script play out against Michigan multiple times, against Georgia, against Clemson, against Notre Dame, against Indiana, against Miami. Different games, different circumstances, different mistakes — but far too often, when Ohio State reaches the most stressful moments of its biggest games, Day's instinct has been to retreat rather than attack.

Despite all of the 10+-win seasons, the 2025 national title, the blowouts against middling to bad teams, this is Buckeye fans' version of "Groundhog Day." We are forced to live this same scenario on repeat again until somehow Ryan Day finally stops seeing his shadow and crawling back into his hole whenever the pressure rises.

While it is never explicitly stated in the movie, director Harold Ramis said that Phil Connors lived that increasingly maddening day in Punxsutawney roughly 12,400 times, the equivalent of about 34 years. It took Bill Murray's character over a third of a century to learn to stop trying to manipulate the day for his own benefit and instead genuinely become a better, more selfless person. I don't know about you, but after all of the stupidity he tried early in the movie, I would hope it wouldn't take me that long to do the right thing.

Obviously, Phil Connors' moral journey is not the same thing as Ryan Day's in-game decision-making, but at some point, I have to hope that the Buckeyes' head coach will decide that losing (and even winning) this way has become too painful and that something has to change.

The nature of college football is that players, coordinators, and position coaches come and go. The head coach is therefore responsible for being the program's anchor, keeping it moored to an identity and philosophy that players and fans can count on year in and year out.

Day has done a remarkable and enviable job of building the Buckeyes into arguably the preeminent program in college football. They are always at the center of the national championship conversation; they never lose games to lesser opponents; they recruit as well as anyone in the country; the roster is stacked with quality human beings you are proud to have representing your institution; few programs prepare players better for the NFL; and yet it still feels like Ohio State has not fully capitalized on everything Day has built.

Now don't get me wrong, despite the fact that every Buckeye fan (and I assume every fan of every major program) enters each season expecting to win the national title, no one legitimately expects them to win the College Football Playoff every year. But we are now in Year 8 of Day's tenure in Columbus, and while we are all obviously giddy and grateful for the one title he brought to Buckeye Nation, it feels like there have been one, two, maybe even three left on the table.

Ohio State had four seasons of arguably the best quarterback play in program history between Justin Fields and C.J. Stroud and never won a title. There have been multiple marquee games in which a single made field goal might have changed everything, and more times than I dare to count when Day — and by extension his team — retreated into a turtle shell, seemingly content to hang on to whatever lead they had and hope for the best.

#Pain pic.twitter.com/hrSiXuJvpa

In many ways, Ryan Day has come to signify greatness in college football. His overall record, his integrity as a leader of young men, and his unwavering dedication to success are all things Buckeye fans should be proud of. But to whom much is given, much is expected. Never losing to Purdue, Northwestern, Nebraska, or Maryland only gets you so far when your own conservative instincts keep surfacing against Michigan, Texas, Indiana, and Miami.

So, here we are again, staring down the same problems that have haunted the Buckeyes numerous times before, and I want to believe this latest collapse will finally be the one to shock Day out of his worst in-game coaching impulses. While I have been critical of Day's decision-making over the years, I have also been very open about how my faith in the program and my belief in him as a human being and a leader continually convince me that this time he might finally figure out how to break free from this vicious cycle that has us seemingly repeating the same day over and over again.

But, oh no, I just had a thought… maybe it's not Ryan Day who is stuck in a never-ending time loop designed to teach him a lesson… maybe it's me who has to finally accept reality in order to break free from this painful pattern.

title: Nets' Julius Randle believes team will exceed expectations this season
description: Brooklyn Nets forward Julius Randle believes that the Nets will exceed the expectations that most people around the league have of them this season.
fullText:
Brooklyn Nets forward Julius Randle surprisingly came to the Nets this offseason after the Minnesota Timberwolves decided to move in a different direction after making it to the Western Conference Semifinals. Brooklyn brought Randle in to improve the team's viability on both ends of the court and the veteran is not backing down from his belief that the Nets can shock the NBA world.

"Whatever your expectations are, whatever expectations that are put upon us, we're gonna exceed them and we're gonna do things at a very high level," Randle said of the Nets this season, according to Andrew Crane of the New York Post. Rookie guard Mikel Brown Jr., whom the Nets selected with the No. 6 overall pick in the 2026 NBA Draft, revealed earlier this summer that Randle's belief in the roster was to the utmost degree.

"We're gonna build, come in with the right habits every single day, and we're gonna do exactly that," Randle continued, per Crane, before addressing what it has been like to be around such a young team. "It was like, actually, kinda refreshing because it was like I lived here for five years but it felt like a fresh start. I was kinda like a newbie again."

Randle was hosting a back-to-school clinic at the Brooklyn Basketball Training Center on Saturday where school supplies were donated to 75 Brooklyn middle-school and high-school students. Randle, 31, is coming off another solid season as he averaged 21.1 points, 6.7 rebounds, and 5.0 assists per game while shooting 48.1% from the field and 31.5% from behind the three-point line.

Most pundits and outlets around the NBA project the Nets to win less 30 games this season despite the addition of Randle, but it seems like his confidence is unaffected by how others see the team. Randle has spoken on what he expects from his partnership with sharpshooting forward Michael Porter Jr. and now, he has doubled down on his belief that Brooklyn will surprise the league this season.

fullText:
Lecce win and bank another massive points in the battle to avoid relegation. After Venezia, Juric's Monza also go down, this time at the Via del Mare.

Watch the full Serie BKT live with LaB Channel on OneFootball: 99 a month!

For the biancorossi, the poor run continues, only partially halted by last week's draw in Parma. Today's defeat, added to those against Inter and Udinese, leaves the Brianzoli in second-to-last place with just one point, alongside Genoa, Parma and Bologna, who still have to play.

Among the teams near the bottom, Juric's side remains one of the most troubled, especially when it comes to defending. Once again today, Lecce score three goals in twenty minutes, two of them from corners. A detail that certainly won't please the former Roma coach.

The Salentini start with their foot on the gas and dominate the first half, taking the lead after just 3 minutes through Lassana Coulibaly, who rises at the back post from Ilic's corner.

Lecce keep pushing and in the 11th minute they double their lead, again from an Ilic corner. This time the scorer changes, with Tiago Gabriel stepping in for his teammate.

At that point Monza realise they have to react and begin to raise their tempo, finding the goal that reopens the game as early as the 20th minute: Birindelli crosses from the right, Robinson creates the space and Mangas pulls one back into an empty net. It seems like the momentum might shift, but Lecce respond again and just a minute later make it 3-1 through Coulibaly, who grabs his brace from close range and, in effect, seems to put the result beyond doubt.

In the second half Monza try to work their way back into the match, but Lecce do brilliantly to contain Juric's side. At least until the 88th minute, when Falcone fumbles an harmless free-kick from Zeballos and ends up knocking the ball into his own net.

The blunder by number 30 sets up a nail-biting finale, with Monza believing again and Lecce pinned back in their own box.

In the end, though, Di Francesco's wall holds firm until the final whistle, which sends the Via del Mare into raptures. Lecce win, take home three massive points and leave Monza five points behind.

title: Position Grades: Temple
description: So, how does one try to grade a game where the final result was fairly comfortable, but the beginning was shaky? Let’s find out! Quarterback: B+ Rocco Becht got off to a rough start, completing only 1 of his first 4 passes (with that one being a beautiful 56-yard bomb to Koby Howard) and seemed […]
fullText:
So, how does one try to grade a game where the final result was fairly comfortable, but the beginning was shaky? Let's find out!

Rocco Becht got off to a rough start, completing only 1 of his first 4 passes (with that one being a beautiful 56-yard bomb to Koby Howard) and seemed to lack the proper touch on his passes and field awareness. However, once he settled down, he went on to complete 20 of his final 23 attempts, including three touchdowns, as PSU strung together five consecutive scoring drives after coming up with nothing on their first three drives.

Carson Hansen got the bulk of the carries this time, picking up 84 yards on 19 rushes. James Peoples also picked up 42 yards on seven carries, and did his best Saquon Barkley impression in the process by hurdling a guy. Cam Wallace even got a touch, but somehow Quinton Martin got zero snaps. Perhaps Martin is banged up or dealing with some other issue, but how he failed to see the field at all after looking like the most complete back out there last week was baffling. I understand why the coaching staff favors Hansen so much, given he's a tough runner who falls forward, but the rushing attack could use a little more explosiveness, even if it has been reasonably efficinet.

Howard was mostly quiet the rest of the game after his initial big catch, but did catch a couple more balls to finish with 68 yards on three catches. Meanwhile, Chase Sowell stepped up, catching five passes for 55 yards, including a screen pass on a critical 3rd down inside the red zone to boost Penn State' s lead to 17-3 in the third quarter and allow the Nittany Lions to start pulling away in this game. Zay Robinson also had a brilliant catch on 3rd and 15 that ultimately led to another scoring drive to put the Nittany Lions up 20-3.

You're going to be hearing Ben Brahmer's name quite a bit this season, and for good reason: Brahmer had a critical, momentum-shifting TD catch with eight seconds to go in the first half and the game tied at three apiece. He also caught the game-sealing TD in the fourth quarter to put PSU up 27-3, en route to a team-high five catches for 79 yards. His uncharacteristic drop on a beautifully-run RPO could have cost PSU a TD but thankfully, Sowell scored on the very next play.

The run blocking left a little more to be desired, but the pass blocking was pretty solid, allowing Becht time to scan the field and find his open receiver.

Yvan Kemajou had PSU's lone sack of the day, as the Nittany Lions were able to get a pass rush going to force Temple QB's Jaxon Smolik and Ajani Sheppard to have to scramble away from trouble. Unfortunately, they didn't do the best job of getting home, as Smolik especially was able to escape and burn the defense with a few big runs, including a 47-yarder that helped set up a field goal in the first half. Considering Temple was missing a few offensive line starters, the D-line didn't dominate the way we hoped.

Tony Rojas once again was the team's top tackler, racking up seven of them. He also had a great interception on Temple's opening drive in the Owls' own red zone that absolutely should have been cashed in by the offense for six points. There were some missed tackles in the early going that allowed Temple to extend drives, but this unit started to clamp down in the second half.

Temple only managed 107 passing yards in this game and that's due in part to some excellent coverage from the secondary. Audavion Collins had multiple pass breakups and this unit as a whole did a tremendous job of getting physical on Temple's receivers without drawing holding or pass interference penalties.

Ryan Barker had a very uncharacteristic shank on what's normally a money distance for him (32 yards). However, he did nail his other two field goals, so I'm not worried about him. Nathan Tiyce once again pinned the Owls deep near their own end zone, while Zay Robinson had a nice 19-yard punt return that had PSU starting from Temple territory (which unfortunately, they couldn't cash in on), and Daryus Dixson got a piece of Temple's field goal attempt in the third quarter that caused it to fall several yards short of the uprights.

Props to the staff for making proper adjustments and not panicking when things weren't go so great early on. At the end of the day, the Nittany Lions ended up taking care of business against an overmatched opponent. That being said, D'Anton Lynn is going to need to figure out how to better contain running QB's and Taylor Mouser might want to start realizing that his team's strength is Rocco slinging the rock to his bevy of wideouts and tight ends and not trying to be a power running team. Some of these issues I imagine can be cleaned up without too much trouble.

Also, was anyone else screaming at the TV for Matt Campbell to burn a freaking timeout right before that TD pass to Brahmer? I imagine that scoring drive is going to show up on the r/nonononoyes subreddit anytime now.

(BONUS CATEGORY) The Traveling Fan Base: A

Shout-out to Nittany Nation for making its presence felt inside Lincoln Financial Field, as they seemingly outnumbered the Temple fans in attendance. The Blue Band also made the trip, which was a nice treat.

title: Alec Pierce expected to be on snap count vs. Ravens
description: Alec Pierce will play against Baltimore, but the Colts will limit his workload in Week 1.
fullText:
Alec Pierce will play for the Colts against the Ravens, but he will not be a full-go in Week 1.

NFL Network's Mike Garafolo reported Sunday morning that Pierce will be on a snap count in Indianapolis' season opener against Baltimore. Garafolo said he does not expect Pierce to handle a full workload and added that one source estimated Pierce would play roughly 20 to 30 snaps.

That would put Pierce below his normal usage, especially for a player expected to have a major role in the Colts' passing game this season. It also lines up with where things have been trending after Pierce missed most of training camp while recovering from ankle surgery.

Pierce was activated off the physically unable to perform list late in camp, giving him a chance to be available for the opener. That was the first important step, but being active and being ready for a full workload are two different things, though, and the Colts appear prepared to manage him carefully in his first game back.

From a football standpoint, Pierce's presence still helps. Even on a limited snap count, his vertical speed forces Baltimore to respect the deep ball and gives Daniel Jones another outside option.

Still, the limited workload is worth watching. Pierce is expected to be one of the Colts' top offensive weapons after a breakout 2025 season, and Indianapolis needs him healthy for the long run. Pushing him too hard in Week 1 would not make much sense if the team believes he is still ramping back up.

For now, the main takeaway is simple: Pierce is available to play against the Ravens, but he isn't 100% yet.

title: NFL "trying all sorts of legal maneuvers" to get Josh Jacobs video
description: Jacobs will remain on paid leave while NFL reviews the case.
fullText:
The regular season opens with Packers running back Josh Jacobs on paid leave. He'll remain there while the NFL determines his punishment under the Personal Conduct Policy after a recent no-contest plea to multiple misdemeanor charges, including battery.

As Ian Rapoport of NFL Network explained on Sunday morning, the NFL will be meeting with Jacobs; that's always part of any review under the Personal Conduct Policy. Per Rapoport, the league also wants to see the video of the altercation, which was captured by a surveillance system in Jacobs's home — and which was placed under seal by the judge presiding over his criminal case.

Rapoport said the league is "trying all sorts of legal maneuvers" to get the video. No specific maneuver was mentioned.

The judge sealed the evidence in the case, including the video, at Jacobs's request. The NFL could, if it wanted, tell Jacobs he won't play until he asks for and receives a reversal of the order his lawyers sought.

Jacobs will receive credit for any games missed while on paid leave. But he won't be playing until the internal review is completed, along with any appeal.

That puts pressure on Jacobs to give the NFL whatever it needs before it can make a decision. It also sets the stage for a negotiated suspension, which would become final once an agreement is reached.

Six games is the baseline suspension for "domestic violence, dating violence, child abuse and other forms of family violence." Aggravating factors can increase the punishment.

Given the league's experiences with the Ray Rice case, it's hard to envision the matter being finalized without the NFL first seeing the video. If a suspension is imposed and the video is later released, it could (depending on the video's contents) creatie a major problem for the league, like the Rice video did in 2014.

title: Rapoport: NFL attempting to get their hands on the Josh Jacobs video
description: Apparently, the NFL hasn’t seen the Josh Jacobs video, either
fullText:
NFL Network/ESPN's Ian Rapoport reported on Sunday morning that the NFL is attempting to obtain the alleged video from the incident that led to Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs being charged with battery and criminal damage to property. Here is what Rapoport said, specifically:

The NFL wants to interview Josh Jacobs. That will happen. They're also trying all sorts of legal maneuvers to try to get the video of the incident that has since been barred by the court. So we'll see if the NFL is able to do that before suspending him.

From @NFLGameDay Morning (in-studio!): The #Falcons won’t have QB Tua Tagovailoa (oblique) today, but Michael Penix Jr could next week or Week 3; Meanwhile, the NFL is attempting to obtain the Josh Jacobs video for its investigation. pic.twitter.com/fqGbuA1Rv8

This video was first mentioned when Jacobs was officially charged by the Brown County District Attorney. According to the police report, the video was obtained via surveillance footage from inside the garage at Jacobs' residence. The county claimed that the video "corroborates the relevant portions of [anonymous victim]'s statement." According to the police report, it shows both Jacobs and the alleged victim leaving and returning to the residence and "the altercation."

Per the county, the victim attempted to leave the residence through the garage, as she believed her calls to the police were not going through due to poor service, and was followed by Jacobs. At that point, Jacobs "grabbed her and threw her to the ground and she struck her head, suffering an injury."

The video apparently confirms that after the victim was on the floor for around 40 seconds, Jacobs returned to the garage to damage the victim's phone — the second phone in the incident, after Jacobs apparently took the first phone from the anonymous woman and left his residence with the phone in his vehicle.

Jacobs pled no contest to the charges of battery and criminal damage to property on Thursday.

In court, District Attorney David Lasse stated that "videos weren't readily accessible on the device and had to be recovered." No further details were given about why a digital forensics unit had to recover the video from the surveillance system.

When the judge stated that he was going to treat pleas of no contest as pleas of guilty, Jacobs confirmed he understood and did not change his plea. When Jacobs was asked by the judge if he believed that the state could prove the elements of battery and the elements of criminal damage to property beyond a reasonable doubt had the case gone to a jury trial and would be "guilty as charged of those offenses," Jacobs also stated, "Yes."

The charge of criminal damage to property was deferred, meaning that it will come off Jacobs' record if he can stay out of the court system for 12 months, avoid contact with the victim, comply with supervision from the Brown County Criminal Justice Services, attend counseling that includes a batterer's prevention program and pay restitution to the victim. If Jacobs can accomplish that, the criminal damage to property charge will be dismissed, but the battery charge will remain on his record regardless. Should Jacobs break any condition of his deferred charge, he could serve up to nine months in jail — as the judge stated that he will sentence Jacobs to the maximum time allowed if it's found that Jacobs has a "material breach" of their agreement after a trial.

Later on that day, Judge Marc Hammer temporarily sealed the evidence in the case, including video recordings, at the request of Jacobs' attorneys.

title: Five-star Brighton crush 10-man Coventry
description: Brighton thrashed 10-man Coventry 5-0 on Sunday to move into fourth place in the Premier League and leave Frank Lampard's side rooted to the bottom of the table.Lampard's men are the only Premier League team without a point this season.
fullText:
Brighton thrashed 10-man Coventry 5-0 on Sunday to move into fourth place in the Premier League and leave Frank Lampard's side rooted to the bottom of the table.

Charalampos Kostoulas put Brighton ahead in the first half and Malick Yalcouye doubled their lead soon after the interval.

Coventry striker Taiwo Awoniyi was sent off for violent conduct in the second half.

Pascal Gross netted from the penalty spot and Lewis Dunk curled home from long-range.

Yasin Ayari wrapped up Brighton's emphatic victory as Coventry's frustrated fans flooded to the exits well before the final whistle.

Coventry are still looking for first Premier League goal since 2001 after going scoreless while losing their first four top-flight matches this season.

Lampard's men are the only Premier League team without a point this season.

The Sky Blues were promoted from the Championship last season to end their 25-year exile from the Premier League.

Brighton are into the top four after winning for the second time this term and the first since their 4-0 rout of Aston Villa on the opening weekend.

Fabian Hurzeler's side should have taken the lead when Jay Dasilva made a hash of an attempted clearance, but the unmarked Diego Gomez lashed just wide from 12 yards.

Coventry threatened through Jack Rudoni but he couldn't keep his header on target from Dasilva's cross.

The same pair nearly combined to put Coventry in front moments later.

Dasilva picked out Rudoni in the Coventry area and the midfielder's cushioned volley forced a superb save from Bart Verbruggen.

Verbruggen made another eye-catching stop to repel Frank Onyeka's volley after the midfielder cleverly flicked the ball up for his shot.

Brighton took the lead in the 35th minute thanks to Kostoulas's inspired moment.

The teenage Greek striker astutely nodded Gross's pass beyond two Coventry defenders and turned to drill a fine finish past Carl Rushworth.

Ephron Mason-Clark squandered a chance to haul Coventry level immediately after the interval, scuffing straight at Verbruggen from close-range.

Yalcouye made Coventry pay for that miss, accelerating away from the defence to double Brighton's advantage with a clinical strike in the 51st minute.

A miserable day for Coventry took a turn for the worse two minutes later when Awoniyi was dismissed for clattering Maxim de Cuyper in the face with his elbow.

Brighton piled on the misery for Lampard, netting for the third time in the 70th minute.

Bobby Thomas's foul on Kostoulas conceded a penalty that Gross slotted home with ease.

Dunk scored the goal of the day in the 83rd minute, curling a spectacular effort into the top corner from 25 yards.

Ayari put the seal on Brighton's rampant performance in stoppage-time as he whipped a composed low strike past Rushworth.

title: Joe Root achieves what no batter has done in 147 years of Test cricket, becomes first batter to score 2,000 fourth-innings runs
description: In an impressive display of skill, Joe Root not only surpassed two thousand runs in fourth innings but also became the first cricketer to net one thousand Test runs at Edgbaston. His unbeaten sixty-two propelled England to victory against Pakistan, marking his sixty-ninth Test fifty—an achievement that puts him ahead of Sachin Tendulkar in the record books. Root continues to break records and redefine Test cricket achievement.
fullText:
Joe Root has added another extraordinary record to his already remarkable Test career, becoming the first player in the 147-year history of Test cricket to cross the 2,000-run mark specifically in the fourth innings. The England star reached the landmark during his unbeaten 62 against Pakistan in the third Test at Edgbaston, producing yet another defining contribution when his team needed him most.

Fourth-innings batting is arguably the ultimate examination of a Test batter. The pitch is often at its most challenging, the target is on the scoreboard and every wicket brings the chasing team closer to defeat.

Root has made that pressure situation his own.

Root's historic achievement came during England's chase of 130 in the third and final Test against Pakistan. The hosts suffered a nightmare beginning, losing Ben Duckett and Emilio Gay in the opening over to slip to 2/2.

With Pakistan suddenly sensing an opportunity to defend a modest target, Root walked into the middle with England under pressure. As has so often been the case throughout his career, the situation appeared to bring out the best in him.

Root steadied the chase alongside Jordan Cox, eventually remaining unbeaten on 62 as England reached 130/2 and completed an eight-wicket victory. Cox also remained unbeaten on 59, with the pair putting together a match-winning partnership after England's early collapse.

The victory completed a 3-0 Test series sweep for England, giving Root the perfect finish to his return to the Test captaincy.

The fourth-innings record was not the only piece of history Root created at Edgbaston. During the same innings, he became the first batter to score more than 1,000 Test runs at the Birmingham venue. Root had entered the match needing 52 runs to reach the landmark, having already accumulated 948 runs at Edgbaston.

Edgbaston is now the fourth Test venue where Root has scored at least 1,000 runs.

His other major haunts are:

That achievement places Root alongside Jacques Kallis and Ricky Ponting as only the third batter to score 1,000 or more Test runs at four different venues.

Root's 62 not out also produced another major milestone. The innings was his 69th Test fifty, moving him to the top of the all-time list for half-centuries. That took him past India's batting great Sachin Tendulkar, who finished his Test career with 68 fifties.

Root now leads the list with 69, followed by Tendulkar on 68 and Shivnarine Chanderpaul on 66. Allan Border and Rahul Dravid have 63 each, while Ricky Ponting has 62. There is another remarkable aspect to that record: Root reached his 69 fifties in fewer Test innings than Tendulkar needed to reach 68.

The 62 not out was also Root's 110th Test innings in which he scored at least 50 runs. That tally includes 41 centuries and 69 fifties, underlining just how consistently he has converted opportunities into substantial scores throughout his career. Reuters confirmed the Edgbaston innings as his 110th Test score of 50 or more.

title: 'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
description: The authorities have struggled to contain the fallout, as frightened migrants flee the country.
fullText:
For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern.

During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses.

"Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home.

"The threats are many… even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten."

President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials.

During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans.

Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country.

"We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food. When those jobs are taken away, the only option left is to return home."

Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.

Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.

"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.

"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.

In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.

She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.

"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.

In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.

Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.

Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.

Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.

He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.

The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.

The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.

Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.

Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.

The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.

Yet observers and those affected argue that it did not have to be this way.

Academic Hesbon Owilla told the BBC the president's comments were bound to be misinterpreted, especially by people who did not have the right documentation.

He says that while the proposed policy is good for Kenya and in line with global migration protocols, the communication about it ought to have been more diplomatic.

For those not in the audience, Owilla says people interpreted the president words as saying: "We are kicking these guys out."

The president did not stop at small-scale traders. A day later, he ordered India's Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local Maasai community in Kajiado county.

Tata has been mining soda ash for years in Lake Magadi, a vast area often covered by a whitish salt crust. The lake's extreme briny environment sustains algae blooms that attract flamboyances of pink flamingos that thrive in the area.

Mining operations began at the lake in 1911 under a British colonial arrangement that is said to have remained largely intact, despite long-running land and resource disputes pitting the company and its predecessors against community and the government.

Economist Odhiambo Ramogi argues that the move to restrict foreign nationals from businesses is too broad - and could do with finessing.

He points out that Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees as well as other migrants, mostly from the EAC region, as well as other international investors.

Ramogi says that Ruto's intention seemed to go beyond "just protecting jobs for Kenyans".

The president's remarks have prompted a wave of support for foreign nationals, including by civil society groups and ordinary Kenyans who have criticised his approach.

In the wake of the criticism, Ruto, who is up for re-election next year, has sought to counter the backlash.

"Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country, protecting opportunities for its citizens, safeguarding the rights of all persons lawfully within its borders," a statement by his spokesman said.

"Kenya's commitment to the East African Community of the African continent remains firm."

Ramogi says that in the end, it is Kenya that stands to lose when citizens of neighbouring countries are targeted.

He points out that Kenya earned $56m (£41m) in exports to Burundi last year, adding that the country would still benefit by allowing competition, as "locking out aliens simply means you don't want a competitive economy that gets to grow a lot faster".

"Now, if you got $56m out of a country, why are you worried about a hawker who's just trying to make, say, $200 in a month?

"It absolutely makes no sense what the president has done."

For Nairobi resident Lima Kabura, whose husband is Tanzanian, the president's remarks were just too hasty. She says he should have first established those who were in the country illegally.

"When they are forced out, I'm left with no work, no business and no husband," she said.

title: Marshall backtracks on support for $5,000 Trump dividend in Kansas Senate debate

fullText:
Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kans.) appeared to shift his opinion on President Trump's $5,000 dividends announced earlier this week.

In a debate at the Kansas State Fair against Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton, a moderator asked both candidates if they supported the dividends, citing the proposal's $1.2 trillion cost amid the growing national debt.

"I'm going to bring in all the information, and then make a decision," he said. "But look, this is not the first time I've disagreed with President Trump, and it probably won't be the last."

"Instead, I said, I'm going to be focused on Kansas jobs. I'm going to be focused on protecting Kansas agriculture and the Kansas cattle industry," he continued.

Marshall's remark comes after his apparent support for the president's proposal in social media post Wednesday.

"Comment how you will spend your $5,000 Trump Dividend when Republicans win in November," he wrote on social platform X.

Marshall, who has Trump's endorsement, has also voiced dissent about Trump administration policy when the president threatened to ban Bombardier, the Canadian jet maker, from selling planes in the U.S., as part of the ongoing trade war with Canada.

"I'm going to fight to keep Bombardier's over 1,200 Kansas jobs. I've already taken that concern inside the Oval Office," Marshall posted on X Tuesday.

The audience at the debate appeared to interrupt Marshall at multiple points in his remarks.

Some attendees chanted "shame on you" while the senator was responding to allegations that his legal team sued over 700 patients when he was a physician resulting in 81 being arrested over outstanding medical debts, according to the New York Times.

"Those are common, common business practices, we would go a year before we would send someone over," he said during the debate, calling the report a "hit job."

Hamilton faces an uphill climb to win in November. A Democrat has not won a Senate race in the Sunflower State since 1932, although the state's two-term Gov. Laura Kelly is a Democrat.

Hamilton's campaign did received a glimmer of hope in August when election handicapper Sabato's Crystal Ball shifted the Kansas Senate race from safe Republican to likely Republican following Hamilton's Democratic primary win.

title: OpenAI's Altman won't do IPO this year, calls AI extinction risk 'unacceptable'
description: OpenAI will not go public in 2026, Chief Executive Sam Altman said in remarks published on Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial
fullText:
LOS ANGELES, Sept 12 (Reuters) - OpenAI will not go public in 2026, Chief Executive Sam Altman said in remarks published on Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence that render "unacceptable" even a 10% risk ‌that AI could cause human extinction by decade's end.

The comments come as more U.S. lawmakers urge new rules to ‌govern AI systems after dire warnings from two researchers from OpenAI rival Anthropic that rapidly progressing AI could lead to the extinction of the human race in ​the not-too-distant future.

"I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don't feel pressure on that," Altman told business magazine Fortune.

Asked if there was a 10% chance of AI-driven extinction, Altman said he did not know how such an estimate could be made, but warned the risk was serious enough that AI companies and governments should ‌act as though it could not be tolerated.

"Whether ⁠it's 10 or eight or six, the point is, we all have a tremendous amount of responsibility, and cannot let egos or incentives for profit or anything else get in the way," Altman added.

"We ⁠need to act such that we are not taking any of those numbers of risk, and I believe we can."

INSTANCES OF AI AGENTS GOING ROGUE

Politicians, both Democrat and Republican, have responded with alarm and calls for more action after cases of AI agents going rogue to hack ​external ​systems and AI safety researchers quitting their companies out of concern at ​the technology risks.

In June, the New York Times said ‌San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off until next year on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO.

At the time, shares in Elon Musk's SpaceX IPO were tumbling after a surge that sent that company's valuation to $1.8 trillion.

Asked by Fortune if an IPO date of 2026 was off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said, "I would say not 2026.

"We got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments ‌can work together."

Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI firms may be ​close to unveiling a pact to slow AI development and work together ​to tackle safety risks, Fortune said.

CALL FOR MORE DELIBERATE APPROACH

On ​Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged AI companies to take a more deliberate approach to development.

"We must ‌slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of ​AI models," Amodei wrote in ​an essay on X.
